stories.title: Israel's Gaza strikes kill up to 22 in a single day — the deadliest stretch in weeks — as mediators warn the ceasefire is at risk
stories.what_happened: Israeli forces struck across Gaza through Sunday night into Monday, killing between **18 and 22 Palestinians** depending on the source, including strikes on a residential tower in Gaza City that killed a family of three, an apartment attack in Khan Younis, and a drone strike on a displacement tent. Gaza's Health Ministry said two additional people died Monday from wounds sustained in earlier attacks. Mediators **Qatar, Egypt, and Turkiye** issued a joint statement Monday strongly condemning the ongoing violations and warning that continued strikes on medical infrastructure threaten to collapse the fragile ceasefire process entirely. The escalation directly follows Hamas's conditional agreement last week to begin disarming, which the Trump administration had described as a diplomatic breakthrough. Analysts note July was already Gaza's deadliest month since the October ceasefire took hold, with 152 people killed.
key_points: Israeli strikes killed as many as **22 Palestinians** across Gaza in the 24 hours to Monday — the **biggest daily death toll in weeks**.
Strikes hit **Gaza City, Deir al-Balah, and Khan Younis**, including residential buildings and a tent for displaced people.
Mediators **Qatar, Egypt and Turkiye** issued a joint statement condemning the violations and warning attacks on medical sites threaten the ceasefire.
**July was Gaza's deadliest month** since the October ceasefire, with **152 Palestinians killed**, per the Hamas-run Health Ministry.
The escalation comes just days after Hamas **conditionally agreed to disarm**, raising doubts about whether Trump's declared peace 'breakthrough' is holding.

depth.background: In late July, Hamas signed a 15-point disarmament framework — agreeing to hand weapons into Palestinian-run, internationally monitored storage — the biggest step yet toward ending nearly two years of war. But Israel never fully signed on, and strikes continued through the window meant to work out implementation. On Sunday, Israeli Energy Minister Eli Cohen publicly said **no deal exists** to stop the attacks and suggested Israel — which already controls about 70% of Gaza — should take the rest.

thread.previously: We reported Israeli strikes had killed nine Palestinians on Sunday, the second straight day of deadly attacks, after Israeli Energy Minister Eli Cohen said publicly that no deal exists to halt them and floated Israel taking full control of Gaza.
thread.changed: The death toll jumped further — up to 22 killed in 24 hours, the worst single day in weeks — and for the first time mediators Qatar, Egypt and Turkiye issued a joint statement condemning the strikes and warning the ceasefire itself is now at risk.

stories.title: Liam Lawson wants his Racing Bulls future settled during F1's summer break, as Red Bull weighs its 2027 lineup
stories.what_happened: Liam Lawson said Monday he expects to have discussions about his Racing Bulls future during the sport's summer break, which runs through August before the season resumes at the Dutch Grand Prix on August 21-23. Lawson has quietly rebuilt his F1 reputation in 2026, finishing his last three races in the points and currently sitting **9th in the drivers' standings with 43 points** alongside highly-rated rookie teammate Arvid Lindblad. His current contract runs out at the end of 2026, and he has previously said he would sign a renewal immediately if the choice were his alone. However, Red Bull's junior team has historically preferred short-term deals that preserve flexibility to promote or swap drivers based on form, meaning Lawson's clarity on 2027 may not arrive as quickly as he'd like despite his on-track improvement.
key_points: **Liam Lawson** says he expects contract talks with **Racing Bulls** to happen during F1's two-week summer break.
He currently sits **9th in the drivers' standings** with **43 points**, his best sustained F1 form to date.
His current deal **expires at the end of 2026**, and he's said he'd sign a renewal **immediately** if it were up to him.
**Red Bull's junior programme** traditionally favors short-term deals, keeping its options open on rising prospects.
The decision affects not just Lawson but the pecking order for **Red Bull's main-team seat** heading into 2027.

depth.background: Lawson was promoted to Red Bull's senior team for part of a previous season but struggled and was moved back down to Racing Bulls (Red Bull's junior/reserve team), then rebuilt his reputation there through 2026. Red Bull operates a two-team system where drivers are shuffled based on performance, and contract calls for the junior team are typically made late and kept short, giving the team flexibility to promote or drop drivers quickly. F1's mandatory two-week summer shutdown — during which teams can't work on car development — is traditionally when driver market talks happen, since team principals and drivers finally have time away from race weekends.

stories.title: Bihar, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh count votes in three assembly bypolls, with Prashant Kishor's Jan Suraaj chasing its first big win in Bankipur
stories.what_happened: Vote counting began at **8am on Monday** under tight security for three assembly bypolls: **Bankipur** in Bihar, **Manjalpur** in Gujarat, and **Datia** in Madhya Pradesh. In Bankipur, Jan Suraaj founder **Prashant Kishor** was ahead of BJP candidate **Neeraj Kumar Sinha**, with his lead widening to **6,011 votes** as counting progressed through multiple rounds — the seat has 31 total rounds scheduled before a final result. In Manjalpur, BJP's **Satish Patel** built an **8,373-vote lead** over Congress's Bhikhabhai Rabari after the fourth round, with Patel polling 12,941 votes to Rabari's 4,568. In Datia, BJP's **Ashutosh Tiwari** led a three-cornered contest after the first round, ahead of Congress's Ghanshyam Singh and the Aazad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram)'s Damodar Yadav 'Mandal'.
key_points: Counting began at **8am today** for bypolls in Bankipur (Bihar), Manjalpur (Gujarat) and Datia (Madhya Pradesh).
In **Bankipur**, Jan Suraaj founder **Prashant Kishor** widened his lead over BJP's Neeraj Kumar Sinha to **6,011 votes**.
In **Manjalpur**, BJP's Satish Patel led Congress by **8,373 votes** after the fourth round of counting.
In **Datia**, BJP's Ashutosh Tiwari led a three-way contest with Congress and the Aazad Samaj Party after round one.
Bankipur is the first real electoral test for Kishor's **Jan Suraaj party**, launched after he built his name as a political strategist.

depth.background: Prashant Kishor is a political strategist who ran high-profile election campaigns for parties including the BJP, Congress and several regional outfits before launching his own party, **Jan Suraaj** ('good governance'), to contest elections in Bihar directly rather than advise others. An assembly bypoll (by-election) is held to fill a seat that falls vacant between general elections, and results are watched closely as an early signal of voter mood. Bankipur is a Patna constituency where Kishor is personally contesting, making this the clearest test yet of whether his years advising other parties translate into votes for his own.

stories.title: Isack Hadjar says Verstappen is 'on a different level' at race management, even as he outqualifies him three times over
stories.what_happened: Isack Hadjar said in comments Monday that while his qualifying pace has been competitive with Verstappen's — he's out-qualified his teammate on **three occasions** this season — the way Verstappen manages a race from start to finish remains 'on a different level.' Hadjar described making 'easy stuff wrong' in-race that Verstappen rarely does, pointing to gaps in tire management, positioning, and race-craft rather than raw speed. Despite showing genuine one-lap pace, Hadjar sits **41 points behind** Verstappen in the championship standings through the first half of his rookie season, missing points finishes in only three grands prix so far — a respectable rookie return, but one that still trails his four-time-champion teammate by a wide margin.
key_points: Red Bull rookie **Isack Hadjar** admits four-time champion **Max Verstappen** is on a **'different level'** in one key skill.
Hadjar says his own one-lap qualifying pace is strong, but Verstappen's **race-day management** is far ahead of his.
Hadjar has actually **out-qualified Verstappen three times** this season, despite the gap in race execution.
He trails his teammate by **41 points** in the drivers' championship so far in his rookie campaign.
Hadjar was promoted from Racing Bulls to Red Bull's senior team for the 2026 season.

depth.background: Hadjar moved up from Red Bull's junior team, Racing Bulls, to partner Verstappen at the main Red Bull team for the 2026 season — a high-pressure seat given Red Bull's history of dropping drivers quickly if they don't perform alongside Verstappen. Verstappen is a four-time world champion widely regarded as one of the best race-day tacticians on the grid, particularly at managing tire wear, defending position, and adapting strategy mid-race — skills distinct from single-lap qualifying speed. Rookies partnering Verstappen have historically struggled to match him over a full season even when they show flashes of raw speed.

stories.title: Lando Norris says F1 is 'the healthiest it's ever been' — even as he keeps criticising the 2026 rules
stories.what_happened: Speaking during F1's summer break, Lando Norris gave his clearest mid-season assessment yet of the sport's new 2026 rules, saying that in terms of where **F1 is as a sport**, 'it's clearly the healthiest it's ever been.' He balanced that with continued criticism of the technical package, saying the regulations are 'a bit of a departure from what's come before' but that the racing itself has produced '**more intense racing, more overtaking and more battles**' than before. In a separate comment picked up the same day, Norris said '**bigger changes will need to come**' before the sport reaches where drivers want it to be, pointing to unresolved issues around the new power units and handling. This follows months of him and other drivers flagging '**superclipping**' — where cars lose electric boost mid-straight — as a problem the FIA has already had to patch mid-season after a scary incident involving Ollie Bearman at Suzuka. Norris said finding 'the right balance' between driver skill and engineering unpredictability is 'where work is ongoing' for the FIA and teams.
key_points: Reigning **2025 world champion** Lando Norris gave F1's radical **2026 rulebook** a mixed mid-season verdict: healthy overall, but still flawed.
He says the new cars deliver '**more intense racing, more overtaking and more battles**' compared to the previous generation.
But he also says '**bigger changes will need to come**' to fix ongoing problems with the new engines and aerodynamics.
The 2026 rules introduced a phenomenon called '**superclipping**', where cars suddenly lose electric power on straights, scrambling overtakes.
Norris currently sits **fifth** in the 2026 drivers' championship, behind leader Kimi Antonelli, despite the praise for his own driving this season.

depth.background: **2026** brought Formula 1's biggest rulebook overhaul in years — all-new, lighter **hybrid power units** with a much bigger share of power coming from electric motors, plus reshaped aerodynamics, all designed to make racing closer and attract new manufacturers like **Cadillac**. The changeover has been rocky: drivers across the grid, including Norris, spent the first half of the season calling the new cars unpredictable and, at times, 'the worst' they'd driven, largely because of a glitch-like effect nicknamed '**superclipping**' where cars abruptly cut electric deployment on long straights. Norris himself won the **2025 title** with McLaren but has struggled relative to expectations in 2026, currently running fifth in the standings as Mercedes rookie Kimi Antonelli leads.

stories.title: IMD issues heavy rain alerts across Delhi, UP, Uttarakhand, Himachal, Punjab and Bihar as monsoon intensifies
stories.what_happened: The **IMD** issued forecasts warning of heavy to very heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds across a broad swath of northern India over the coming days. **Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Jammu & Kashmir** are forecast to see the heaviest rain, continuing through **August 7**, with isolated spots at risk of very heavy downpours. **Delhi, Haryana and Punjab** are expected to see heavy rain between **August 2 and 4**, while **east Uttar Pradesh** and **Bihar** are under alert into **August 5-6**. The IMD has specifically warned that intense rainfall could trigger **flash floods, waterlogging, and landslides**, and it has advised tourists and pilgrims heading to Himalayan states to check conditions before traveling.
key_points: The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** has forecast heavy to very heavy rain across northern India over the next several days.
**Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Jammu & Kashmir** are expected to get heavy-to-very-heavy rain through **August 7**.
**Delhi, Haryana and Punjab** face heavy rain risk between **August 2 and 4**.
**East Uttar Pradesh** and **Bihar** are under alert for heavy rainfall into **August 5-6**.
Authorities have warned of **flash floods, waterlogging and landslides** in vulnerable and hilly areas.

depth.background: India's economy and daily life run on the **southwest monsoon** — the seasonal rains from June to September that supply most of the country's annual rainfall, water its farms, and refill its reservoirs. But the same monsoon that India depends on for agriculture also regularly turns destructive, especially in the Himalayan foothills where heavy rain triggers landslides, and in low-lying northern plains prone to flash flooding. This alert comes as several parts of India — Assam, Kerala, and Gujarat among them — are already dealing with deadly flood and landslide damage this monsoon season, so northern India's IMD warning adds another front to an already stretched disaster-response season.

stories.title: A bomb rips through a Moscow restaurant, killing 5 — Russia blames Ukraine
stories.what_happened: An explosive device detonated inside Balzi Rossi, an Italian restaurant in central Moscow, on the night of **Saturday, August 1, 2026**, killing **5 people** and injuring **19** others. Several Russian media outlets reported — without official confirmation — that the bombing targeted a Russian general who was celebrating his birthday at the restaurant, with some naming **Col.-Gen. Alexander Chaiko**, who recently took over as chief of Russia's aerospace forces. On **August 3**, the Russian Embassy in Rome issued a statement blaming **"Kyiv terrorists"** for the attack, saying it was meant to intimidate the Italian community working in Russia by showing they "too are in the crosshairs." Ukrainian authorities have not responded publicly to the accusation. No group has claimed responsibility, and the identity of the intended target — if there was one — remains unconfirmed.
key_points: An improvised explosive device tore through **Balzi Rossi**, an Italian restaurant in central Moscow, on **Saturday night**, killing **5 people** and wounding **19**.

Russian media claim the real target was a senior military officer — some outlets name **Col.-Gen. Alexander Chaiko**, newly appointed chief of Russia's aerospace forces, who was reportedly celebrating his birthday there.
Russia's embassy in Rome accused **"Kyiv terrorists"** of trying to scare Italians working in Russia into thinking they too could become targets.
**Ukraine has not commented**, and no independent source has confirmed who planted the device or who — if anyone — was the intended target.
The blast fits a **recurring pattern** of unexplained explosions and fires inside Russia that Moscow routinely, and often without hard proof, blames on Ukrainian sabotage.

depth.background: Russia and Ukraine have been at war since **February 2022**, and since then Russian territory has periodically been hit by explosions, fires, and drone strikes that Moscow attributes to Ukrainian intelligence operations — a form of sabotage warfare that runs alongside the front-line fighting. Foreign nationals, including Italians, still live and work in Russia despite Western sanctions and the diplomatic rupture between Moscow and most of Europe. The restaurant, Balzi Rossi, is an upscale Italian venue in central Moscow, and Saturday's bombing happened while it was full of weekend diners. Russian officials have a long history of publicly blaming Kyiv for domestic incidents within hours, often before any investigation is complete.

stories.title: Delhi court acquits former wrestling federation chief Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh in the sexual harassment case brought by six women wrestlers
stories.what_happened: On Monday, August 3, Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Ashwini Panwar of the Rouse Avenue Court in Delhi pronounced the verdict at 10:30am, acquitting Singh of all charges brought by the six adult women wrestlers. The original FIR had cited IPC sections covering assault or criminal force intended to outrage a woman's modesty, sexual harassment, stalking, and common intention. This acquittal is separate from — and follows — an earlier, related case involving a minor wrestler, in which Singh had already received relief after police filed a closure report accepted by the court.
key_points: A Delhi court **acquitted** ex-WFI chief **Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh** of sexually harassing **six women wrestlers**
The verdict was delivered **Monday at 10:30am** by the Rouse Avenue Court, closing a three-year legal battle
Charges had included **outraging a woman's modesty, sexual harassment, and stalking** under since-replaced IPC sections
Singh had **separately been cleared** in a related case involving a minor wrestler after police filed a closure report

depth.background: Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh headed the Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) when, in 2023, a group of India's most decorated wrestlers — including Olympic and world medalists — accused him of sexual harassment during his tenure. Their allegations triggered a prolonged, high-profile sit-in protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar that drew national attention to how women athletes are treated within Indian sports federations. Police eventually filed charges against Singh under the old Indian Penal Code, and the case has moved through pre-trial hearings, bail applications, and the trial itself over the past three years.

stories.title: Punjab Kings vice-captain Shashank Singh quits Chhattisgarh for Puducherry over 'disrespect'
stories.what_happened: Shashank Singh has left **Chhattisgarh** to represent **Puducherry** from the **2026-27 domestic season**, after the Chhattisgarh State Cricket Sangh (CSCS) issued him the NOC he needed to switch states. Singh told ESPNcricinfo the association gave him **no explanation** for excluding him from the **2026 Chhattisgarh Cricket Premier League** squad, and did not tell him why he was also missing from the **conditioning camp** for state probables. He said he had spent much of the past year managing a **shoulder injury and a fractured finger** and felt the board failed to support him through that recovery, adding that someone who won a **BCCI domestic award** deserves 'clarity, not ridicule'. Puducherry has agreed to let him play **white-ball cricket only** for now while he continues managing his fitness. The switch comes only months after Singh was made Punjab Kings' vice-captain in the IPL, raising his public profile just as his domestic-team relationship collapsed.
key_points: Shashank Singh, Punjab Kings' **vice-captain** and the **2023-24 BCCI best domestic white-ball all-rounder**, has left Chhattisgarh for **Puducherry**.
He was dropped from the **2026 Chhattisgarh Cricket Premier League** squad with **no explanation** given.
Singh says the state association gave him **no support** while he recovered from a shoulder injury and a fractured finger.
He will play **white-ball cricket only** this season while he keeps managing his fitness.
The **Chhattisgarh State Cricket Sangh** issued him a **No-Objection Certificate (NOC)** to make the move official.

depth.background: Shashank Singh spent most of a long domestic career representing **Chhattisgarh**, a relatively young state cricket association carved out after the state's 2000 formation, before an explosive **2023 IPL season with Punjab Kings** turned him into a household name and, eventually, the franchise's **vice-captain**. He was named the **BCCI's best domestic white-ball all-rounder for 2023-24**, one of Indian domestic cricket's more prestigious individual honours. Players switch states in Indian domestic cricket occasionally and always need a **No-Objection Certificate (NOC)** from their current association, but a contracted IPL player of Singh's profile walking away is unusual and signals a real breakdown in the player-association relationship, not a routine transfer.

stories.title: ITC's profit falls 15.6% even as revenue jumps 27% — cigarettes-to-hotels giant flags West Asia disruption
stories.what_happened: ITC reported **consolidated revenue of ₹29,523.30 crore** and **net profit of ₹4,508.79 crore** for the quarter ended June 2026 (Q1 FY27), a **15.61% decline** in profit from ₹5,343.41 crore in the same quarter last year, even as gross revenue from products and services climbed nearly **28%** to ₹29,409.82 crore. Total income for the quarter came in at ₹30,179.01 crore. ITC attributed the profit squeeze to a combination of factors: the impact of its Sproutlife Foods acquisition affecting year-on-year comparability, and heightened uncertainty from the ongoing **conflict in West Asia**, which triggered a sharp rise and volatility in crude oil and crude-linked input prices along with broader trade and supply-chain disruptions. The results were released as part of India's heaviest earnings week of the quarter, with more than 600 companies reporting results between August 3 and 8.
key_points: ITC's **consolidated net profit fell 15.6%** to **₹4,508.79 crore** for the June quarter (Q1 FY27), down from ₹5,343.41 crore a year earlier.
Revenue rose sharply to **₹29,523.30 crore**, with gross revenue from sale of products and services at ₹29,409.82 crore — up nearly **28%** year-on-year.
The **revenue-up, profit-down** mismatch signals margins got squeezed even as sales grew.
ITC pointed to **volatile, higher crude oil prices** and **supply-chain disruption** linked to the ongoing conflict in **West Asia**, plus one-off effects from its Sproutlife Foods acquisition.
The results land in the middle of India's **busiest earnings week**, with over 600 companies — including LIC, SBI and Bharti Airtel — reporting through August 8.

depth.background: ITC is one of India's largest conglomerates, built originally on cigarettes but now spanning hotels, packaged foods, paperboard/packaging, and agri-business — its cigarette division has historically been a cash-generating anchor that funds expansion into these other, lower-margin businesses. As a heavyweight Sensex and Nifty constituent, ITC's quarterly results are watched as a bellwether for consumer demand and cost pressures across India's FMCG (fast-moving consumer goods) sector. This quarter's numbers are also harder to compare cleanly with last year because ITC recently folded in its acquisition of Sproutlife Foods, and because global crude markets have been unusually volatile due to the West Asia conflict.

stories.title: Fire engulfs Bihar passenger train engine and coaches; all evacuated safely
stories.what_happened: Around 3:25 AM on Monday, train 63344 — the Samastipur-Saharsa passenger service — arrived at Platform 2 of Simri Bakhtiyarpur station when the station master noticed flames near the train's **motor engine**. The fire spread quickly to an adjoining coach and then to a third, eventually engulfing three coaches in total. Station staff and passengers moved quickly to evacuate everyone on board, and no one was hurt. Because the flames could not be controlled with onboard fire extinguishers, the local fire station dispatched multiple fire tenders, including a foam tender and a water tender, which brought the fire fully under control by **5:50 AM** — roughly two and a half hours after it started. Train movement on the section was disrupted for about two hours, delaying connecting services including the Kosi Express, Janaki Express and a Shravani special train. Railway officials have suspected a short circuit but have ordered a formal inquiry to pin down the exact cause.
key_points: Fire broke out in the engine and spread to **three coaches** of the Samastipur-Saharsa passenger train (No. **63344**) at Simri Bakhtiyarpur station in Bihar's Saharsa district around **3:25 AM**.
All passengers were evacuated safely — **no injuries or casualties** reported.
Fire tenders took roughly **two-and-a-half hours** to fully douse the blaze, which was brought under control by **5:50 AM**.
Railway officials suspect a **short circuit** as the cause; an official inquiry has been ordered to confirm it.
Several other services on the route — including the Kosi Express and Janaki Express — were **delayed** as the line was cleared.

depth.background: Simri Bakhtiyarpur is a station on the Samastipur-Saharsa passenger corridor in north Bihar, a route served by older-generation coaches that run frequently through the state's rural heartland. Coach and engine fires on Indian Railways — one of the world's largest rail networks, moving tens of millions of passengers a day — are almost always traced back to **electrical faults** rather than sabotage, and this is not the first such incident on Bihar's rail lines this year. Quick-response fire tenders and platform evacuation drills are the frontline defence against such incidents turning deadly, as tragic derailments and fires in the past have shown how fast a rail fire can escalate.

stories.title: A magnitude-5.3 earthquake rattles Egypt, shaking felt from Suez to Cairo and across five countries
stories.what_happened: The USGS recorded a **magnitude-5.3 earthquake** at roughly **3:00am local time on Monday, August 3**, centered about **41 kilometers north-northeast of Suez** at a shallow depth of **10 kilometers**. The shallow depth meant the shaking was felt more strongly at the surface than a deeper quake of the same magnitude would produce. Residents reported feeling tremors not just in nearby Cairo but as far away as **Cyprus, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, and Saudi Arabia** — a sign of how shallow Mediterranean-region quakes can radiate over long distances. As of the latest reports, **no injuries, deaths, or structural damage** have been confirmed. Magnitude estimates varied slightly across monitoring agencies (from 5.0 to 5.7), which is typical in the first hours before readings are fully calibrated.
key_points: A **magnitude-5.3 earthquake** struck **41km northeast of Suez, Egypt** at around **3am local time** on Monday.
The quake had a shallow depth of just **10km** — shallow quakes shake the surface harder than deep ones of the same size.
Tremors were felt as far as **Cairo, Cyprus, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Saudi Arabia**.
No casualties or structural damage have been reported so far, per the **US Geological Survey (USGS)**.
Different agencies reported slightly different magnitudes (5.0 to 5.7) — normal in the first hours after a quake.

depth.background: Egypt sits near the boundary where the **African and Arabian tectonic plates** are slowly pulling apart, a zone that includes the Gulf of Suez and the Red Sea. This makes the region seismically active, though damaging earthquakes are relatively rare in Egypt compared to neighbors like Turkey or Iran. The Gulf of Suez area has a history of moderate quakes, including a similarly sized one in 2020, but Cairo's dense, older building stock makes even a distant, moderate quake a source of public anxiety.

stories.title: Cuba's power grid collapses for the 6th time in 2026, plunging the island into darkness again
stories.what_happened: Cuba's state-owned electricity utility announced on social media that the national grid **collapsed late Sunday night**, plunging the entire island of roughly **10 million people** into darkness. It is the **sixth nationwide blackout Cuba has suffered in 2026**, following two in March and three more in July, making this one of the worst years for grid failures in recent memory. The immediate cause is the same each time: aging power plants running short of fuel oil, worsened by the loss of Venezuelan oil shipments after the US captured Maduro in January and the acting Venezuelan government stopped sending fuel to Havana. State media said crews began restoring power gradually on **Monday afternoon**, region by region, though past collapses have taken multiple days for full service to return. The US Embassy in Havana has warned American travelers to Cuba to prepare for major disruptions.
key_points: Cuba's national electrical grid collapsed late **Sunday, August 2**, cutting power to the entire island of **about 10 million people**.
It's the **6th nationwide blackout** Cuba has suffered in 2026 alone, after two in March and three in July.
The crisis is tied to a **years-long fuel shortage**, worsened by continued **US pressure on oil shipments** to Cuba.
The shortage deepened after the US captured Venezuelan president **Nicolás Maduro** in January, cutting off oil shipments Cuba relied on.
State media said crews began **restoring power Monday afternoon**, though full recovery from past collapses has taken days.

depth.background: Cuba's state-run electrical grid runs on aging, Soviet-era power plants that depend heavily on imported fuel oil, much of which historically came from close ally **Venezuela**. The island has been in a **years-long energy crisis**, with blackouts becoming a near-routine part of life as plants break down faster than they can be repaired or fueled. The US has long maintained a trade embargo on Cuba and has ramped up pressure on oil shipments to the island. The crisis worsened sharply after US forces captured Venezuelan President **Nicolás Maduro** in January 2026, disrupting the Venezuelan oil shipments that had helped keep Cuba's grid limping along.

stories.title: USA cricketer Akhilesh Reddy banned for eight years over Abu Dhabi T10 match-fixing
stories.what_happened: The ICC's Anti-Corruption Tribunal found **Akhilesh Reddy** guilty on **three counts** of the Anti-Corruption Code over his conduct during the **2025 Abu Dhabi T10 League**. The tribunal ruled that he approached a teammate — referred to as 'Player A' — and asked him to **'give runs'**, meaning deliberately bowl in a way that concedes extra runs, allegedly at the behest of team management. When that player refused and instead reported the approach to the ICC's Anti-Corruption Unit, he was **dropped from the playing XI** shortly before the match in question. Reddy was also found to have **obstructed the investigation** by deleting relevant messages and call logs from his mobile phone once it began. His **eight-year ban is backdated to 21 November 2025**, the date of his provisional suspension, meaning he will not be eligible to return until **2033**.
key_points: USA international **Bodugum Akhilesh Reddy**, 26, has been banned from all cricket for **eight years**.
The ICC's Anti-Corruption Tribunal found him guilty over conduct during the **2025 Abu Dhabi T10 League**.
He asked a teammate to **'give runs'** — deliberately concede extra runs while bowling — allegedly on behalf of team management.
That teammate refused and instead **reported him to the ICC's Anti-Corruption Unit**, and was dropped from the XI as a result.
Reddy also **deleted messages and call logs** from his phone in an attempt to obstruct the investigation.

depth.background: The **Abu Dhabi T10** is a short, fast franchise tournament in the UAE that has repeatedly drawn scrutiny from cricket's anti-corruption authorities, because its **compressed matches, lower player profiles and heavy betting-market interest** make it an attractive target for fixers looking for less scrutiny than bigger leagues get. The **ICC Anti-Corruption Unit (ACU)** monitors global franchise leagues for approaches to players, officials and support staff, and has banned other players and even support-staff members from past T10 editions. Reddy, an Indian-origin American cricketer, was **provisionally suspended in November 2025** while the ICC investigated, and the case has now concluded with a tribunal verdict finding him guilty.

stories.title: Fast-moving wildfires destroy 700+ structures and force 65,000 to evacuate around Spokane, Washington
stories.what_happened: Three wildfires tore through the Spokane, Washington area starting **Saturday, August 1**, destroying **more than 700 structures** combined — the Old Trails Fire alone accounted for **640** of them — and forcing roughly **65,000 people** to evacuate. The Spokane Convention Center became the main overnight shelter, housing **409 families** who fled their homes with little notice. By Sunday evening, about **12 square miles** of terrain had burned around the city. Spokane Mayor **Lisa Brown** called it **'the worst natural disaster our region has faced,'** and officials warned there is still 'potential for lives to be lost' as search-and-damage assessment continues. High winds and hot, dry conditions have made the fires fast-moving and hard to contain.
key_points: Three fires — the **Old Trails Fire**, Fairview Fire, and Autumn Lane Fire — are burning around Spokane.
More than **700 structures** have been destroyed; officials haven't yet said how many were homes.
About **65,000 people** have been ordered to evacuate across Spokane County.
Roughly **12 square miles** have burned as of the latest count, fueled by high winds and hot, dry weather.
Spokane's mayor called it **'the worst natural disaster our region has faced.'**

depth.background: Spokane is Washington state's **second-largest city**, sitting in the state's dry, forested eastern half — a region that, like much of the western US, has seen its wildfire season grow longer and more destructive over the past decade as summers get hotter and drier. The **Old Trails Fire broke out on Saturday, August 1**, and two more fires (Fairview and Autumn Lane) ignited nearby soon after, all fanned by strong winds that let them jump from wildland into residential neighborhoods with little warning. The cause of the fires has not yet been determined.

stories.title: Harmanpreet Kaur keeps India Women's captaincy as BCCI names Asia Cup 2026 squad
stories.what_happened: The **BCCI (Board of Control for Cricket in India)** announced a **15-player squad** for the 2026 Women's Asia Cup, retaining **Harmanpreet Kaur as captain** and **Smriti Mandhana as vice-captain**. The full squad includes Shafali Verma, Jemimah Rodrigues, Bharati Fulmali, Deepti Sharma, wicketkeepers Richa Ghosh and G. Kamalini, Arundhati Reddy, Prema Rawat, Radha Yadav, Sree Charani, Renuka Thakur, Nandini Sharma and Kranti Gaud. The board separately named an **India A squad** for the ACC Rising Stars Asia Cup, a parallel tournament for emerging players, giving several uncapped players — including Radha Yadav as captain of that side — a shot at senior selectors' attention.
key_points: BCCI announced a **15-member squad** for the 2026 Women's Asia Cup.
**Harmanpreet Kaur** retains the captaincy; **Smriti Mandhana** stays vice-captain.
Squad includes Shafali Verma, Jemimah Rodrigues, Deepti Sharma, and wicketkeeper **Richa Ghosh**.
India go in as **defending stakes-holders**, aiming to reclaim the continental crown.
A separate **India A squad** was also named for the ACC Rising Stars Asia Cup.

depth.background: The **Women's Asia Cup** is the region's top continental cricket title, contested by India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and other Asian sides. India has traditionally been the dominant side but has faced tougher competition in recent editions as rivals like Sri Lanka and Bangladesh have improved. **Harmanpreet Kaur** has captained India Women through a period of rising expectations, including a maiden T20 World Cup near-miss, while **Smriti Mandhana** remains the team's most consistent batting star.

stories.title: F1 delays its 2027 calendar release as the Iran war leaves this year's Gulf finale in doubt
stories.what_happened: F1 announced it will **delay publishing its full 2027 calendar until autumn**, rather than releasing it on its usual earlier schedule, while it waits to see whether the fragile Middle East peace process holds. The uncertainty is severe enough that it's not yet clear whether even this year's planned **season-ending Qatar and Abu Dhabi races** can proceed as scheduled — after Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were already cancelled earlier in 2026 because of the Iran war. F1's tentative plan is for **Bahrain to host the 2027 season opener** on March 14, followed by Saudi Arabia on March 21, with a single pre-season test in Bahrain in late February — but organizers are keeping alternative venues in reserve in case the Gulf situation doesn't stabilize. Tyre supplier Pirelli says it needs a **minimum seven weeks' notice** to ship tyres to a race, which effectively forces F1 to lock in where pre-season testing and the opening races will happen by the **middle of January 2027** at the latest.
key_points: F1 will hold back its full **2027 calendar** release until **autumn** instead of the usual earlier date.
The **Iran war** has already forced F1 to cancel this year's **Bahrain and Saudi Arabia** races.
It's now unclear whether the **Qatar and Abu Dhabi** season finale can go ahead as planned.
The tentative 2027 plan still has **Bahrain hosting the season opener** on March 14.
Tyre supplier **Pirelli needs 7 weeks' notice** to ship tyres, forcing F1 toward a decision by mid-January.

depth.background: F1's calendar has leaned heavily on the **Middle East** in recent years — Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi have all hosted races, often for lucrative hosting fees that help fund the wider championship. That regional cluster is now caught in the fallout of the broader **Iran war** that has destabilized parts of the Gulf this year, which already forced F1 to scrap the Bahrain and Saudi Arabia rounds from the 2026 calendar. F1 typically confirms next year's calendar well before the current season ends, so teams, broadcasters and host countries can plan logistics, but this year that timeline itself has become a casualty of the regional instability.

stories.title: Rahul Gandhi calls delimitation a 'BJP conspiracy' to strip Tamil Nadu of power — Congress backs him, BJP hits back
stories.what_happened: Speaking in **Chennai on Saturday**, Congress's Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, **Rahul Gandhi**, said the BJP-led Centre's planned delimitation exercise was **'designed to disenfranchise people and take away the political power of the people of Tamil Nadu,'** calling it a **'BJP conspiracy.'** He called on political parties nationwide — especially in Tamil Nadu — to unite in opposition, warning that anyone who backs delimitation would be 'betraying Tamil Nadu.' By Monday, **Congress had formally thrown its weight behind Gandhi's position**, while the **BJP hit back**, rejecting the characterization and defending the government's approach. The dispute centers on the fact that Lok Sabha seat numbers have been **frozen since the 1971 Census** specifically to stop faster-growing northern states gaining seats at the expense of southern states that slowed population growth — a freeze due to lift after the next census.
key_points: Gandhi calls the planned delimitation **'designed to disenfranchise'** Tamil Nadu
He urges **all parties**, especially in Tamil Nadu, to unite against it
Congress has now **officially backed** Gandhi's stand; BJP has hit back
Lok Sabha seat numbers have been **frozen since the 1971 Census**
Southern states fear losing **relative seat share** once the freeze lifts after the next census

depth.background: India's Lok Sabha (the lower house of Parliament) allocates seats to states roughly by population. Because southern states like Tamil Nadu succeeded early at slowing population growth — largely through better health and education outcomes — while northern states grew faster, a straight population-based reallocation would shrink the South's seat share and grow the North's. To avoid punishing states for good policy, Parliament **froze seat numbers based on the 1971 Census**, and that freeze has been extended repeatedly, currently due to lift after the first census conducted post-2026. 'Delimitation' is the technical term for this seat-redrawing exercise, and it has been a live political fear in the South for years, since losing seats means losing a say in national policy and funding.

stories.title: Justin Greaves steadies West Indies to 239/5 as spin bowling dominates Day 2 in Trinidad
stories.what_happened: On **Day 2**, West Indies extended their overnight position to **239 for 5** by the time bad light stopped play, taking the upper hand on a spin-dominated day. **Justin Greaves** batted through the innings unbeaten for a fighting half-century, combining with **Roston Chase** for an unbroken **66-run partnership** that pushed the total past 200 with five wickets still in hand. Pakistan's spin duo, **Usman and Sajid**, bowled in tandem for long stretches and kept West Indies pinned down, but couldn't find the breakthroughs they needed — every West Indies batter in the lineup reached double figures, denying Pakistan the cheap dismissals needed to build pressure. Day 1 had already been disrupted by rain, during which Pakistan dropped seasoned pacer Mohammad Abbas from the XI, a call that drew scrutiny given his experience.
key_points: West Indies reach **239/5** with **5 wickets in hand** after Day 2
**Justin Greaves** unbeaten on a fighting half-century, an unbroken **66-run stand** with Roston Chase
Pakistan's spin pair **Usman and Sajid** stifled West Indies for long periods
Every West Indies batter reached **double figures** — no cheap wickets for Pakistan
This is the **series-deciding 2nd Test** at Trinidad's Queen's Park Oval

depth.background: Pakistan is touring the West Indies for a **two-match Test series**, with the second and final Test at Trinidad's Queen's Park Oval running **August 2-6**. Day 1 was disrupted by rain and marked by Pakistan's decision to drop veteran fast bowler **Mohammad Abbas**, with West Indies closing on **165 for 3**. Because this is the series decider, every session carries extra weight for both sides.

thread.previously: Day 1 was disrupted by rain, and Pakistan's decision to drop experienced seamer Mohammad Abbas drew scrutiny; West Indies closed on 165 for 3.
thread.changed: West Indies extended their position to 239 for 5, with Justin Greaves batting through for an unbeaten half-century and every batter reaching double figures against tight Pakistan spin.

stories.title: The FIA reveals why it couldn't fix F1's messy 2026 engine rules before the season started
stories.what_happened: The FIA has publicly explained why it couldn't fix known problems with F1's 2026 engine rules before the season began, despite seeing the issues coming. Under the **Power Unit Advisory Committee framework**, any substantial rule change requires support from the FIA, Formula One Management, and **at least four of the five power-unit manufacturers** — and when the FIA proposed adjustments, **four manufacturers rejected them**. The FIA says it tried: at a 2025 meeting in Bahrain, it proposed moving to a **60/40 power split** between combustion and electric power, but the plan was voted down. After pre-season testing exposed further problems, the FIA did push through one fix — cutting maximum energy deployment during races from **350kW to 200kW** — but broader concerns about how predictable and exciting the racing is have persisted through the season.
key_points: A rule change needed sign-off from the **FIA, F1, and at least 4 of 5** engine manufacturers
Four manufacturers **rejected** a proposed **60/40 power split** fix floated in 2025
The FIA did push through one change: cutting max deployment from **350kW to 200kW**
The governance deal locks in engine rules the way the **Concorde Agreement** locks in team rules
Drivers have complained all season about **energy management and safety** under the new rules

depth.background: Formula 1 introduced a major new engine (power unit) rulebook for **2026**, aimed at cutting costs and increasing electric power, but the change has been rocky — drivers have spent the season complaining about how the cars manage energy deployment and about safety in certain conditions. When a manufacturer signs up to build F1 engines, it agrees to a binding **governance agreement** with the FIA (motorsport's regulator) and Formula One Management — similar to how the **Concorde Agreement** binds the teams. That agreement sets a high bar for changing rules once set, which is exactly what tied the FIA's hands here.

stories.title: Palantir reports Q2 earnings today, testing whether its AI-fueled rally can survive a 40% stock pullback
stories.what_happened: Palantir is due to report **second-quarter 2026 earnings today**, with analysts expecting roughly **$1.81 billion in revenue** and **$0.34 earnings per share**. It enters the report on an eight-quarter streak of beating Wall Street's estimates — most recently topping Q1 2026 expectations of $0.27 EPS with an actual $0.33. That first-quarter report showed **85% year-over-year revenue growth**, powered by **133% growth in US commercial revenue** and 84% growth in government revenue. Yet even with that growth, Palantir shares have fallen roughly **40% from their peak**, and options markets are pricing in a swing of about **12%** in either direction once results land — a sign investors are deeply split on whether the valuation still makes sense.
key_points: Palantir reports **Q2 2026 results today**, with Wall Street expecting **$1.81 billion revenue** and **$0.34 EPS**
The company has beaten earnings estimates for **eight straight quarters**
Q1 2026 revenue grew **85% year-over-year**, with **US commercial revenue up 133%**
The stock is still down **~40% from its all-time high**, and options markets price in a **12% swing** on today's results

depth.background: Palantir builds data-analysis and AI software used heavily by **US government and defense agencies**, and increasingly by large commercial clients. It became one of the most-watched **AI-boom stocks** of the past two years, with its share price climbing far faster than its revenue — which made it a lightning rod in the debate over whether AI stocks are overvalued. The stock has since pulled back sharply from its highs even as the underlying business kept growing fast, reflecting investor nervousness about **how much future growth is already priced in**.

stories.title: Lok Sabha passes bill to expand the Supreme Court from 34 to 38 judges
stories.what_happened: The Lok Sabha (India's lower house of Parliament) passed the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026** by voice vote today, formally raising the court's **sanctioned judge strength from 33 to 37**, excluding the Chief Justice of India — taking the court's total possible complement from **34 to 38 judges**. The bill converts into permanent law an ordinance the President had already promulgated in May 2026, under which the additional judges may already have begun functioning. The bill still needs to clear the Rajya Sabha (upper house) to complete its passage through Parliament. Government ministers framed the move as necessary to help the court clear its backlog faster.
key_points: The **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026** passed the Lok Sabha by voice vote today
It raises the sanctioned strength of judges from **33 to 37**, excluding the Chief Justice — taking the full court from **34 to 38**
The change follows an **ordinance the President promulgated in May 2026**, which this bill now formally enacts into law
More sanctioned judges means **more benches can sit at once**, not that any single case gets more judges

depth.background: India's Supreme Court has repeatedly had its judge count raised over the decades as its case backlog has grown — the court now hears an enormous volume of appeals and constitutional matters each year. This particular expansion was first put into effect quickly via a **presidential ordinance in May 2026** (a temporary law the government can issue between parliamentary sessions), and the Monsoon Session's job was to formally convert that ordinance into a lasting **Act of Parliament**. The bill amends the original **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956**.

stories.title: India's official industrial output grows 7.3% in June — the fastest pace in nearly two years
stories.what_happened: India's **Index of Industrial Production (IIP)** rose **7.3% year-on-year in June 2026**, accelerating sharply from **5.0% growth in May** and marking the **fastest pace of industrial growth in nearly two years**. Within the index, **manufacturing output grew 7.8%** and **electricity and gas supply grew 10.6%**, while mining lagged. Of the 23 manufacturing industry groups tracked, **19 posted positive growth**, with **electrical equipment (+34%)**, **motor vehicles and trailers (+17.5%)**, and **food products (+10.8%)** the top contributors. The IIP's index level stood at **123.1**, up from 114.7 a year earlier.
key_points: The **Index of Industrial Production (IIP)** grew **7.3% year-on-year in June**, up from 5.0% in May
**Manufacturing grew 7.8%** and **electricity & gas supply grew 10.6%**
**19 of 23 manufacturing industry groups** posted positive growth
Electrical equipment (**+34%**), motor vehicles (**+17.5%**) and food products (**+10.8%**) led the gains

depth.background: The **IIP** is India's official, government-compiled measure of actual factory, mining, and utility output — different from (and more backward-looking than) the private **PMI survey** the market already saw for July, which showed manufacturing sentiment cooling. The two aren't contradictory: IIP measures hard output data for **June**, a month earlier than the PMI's forward-looking July survey. Industrial output growth had been soft through much of the year, so June's jump is a notable acceleration.

stories.title: Alibaba's new Qwen3.8-Max AI model claims to match Anthropic's Claude — and its stock jumps 7%
stories.what_happened: Alibaba unveiled **Qwen3.8-Max** on August 3, a multimodal model that reads text, images and video, built on **2.4 trillion** total parameters with only around 95 billion activated per request. On benchmark tests it scored competitively with or ahead of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Fable 5 on coding-heavy tests like Terminal-Bench 2.1 and PaperBench, though it lagged on some broader reasoning tests and OpenAI's top model. The model supports a **1-million-token** context window, letting it process roughly a 750,000-word document in a single pass. Alibaba priced access at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens — undercutting many Western rivals — and said full weights would be open-sourced on Hugging Face and ModelScope within a week. Investors reacted immediately, sending Alibaba's shares up as much as **7%**.
key_points: Alibaba released Qwen3.8-Max, its biggest-ever AI model, built on **2.4 trillion** parameters, with only about **95 billion** active per question
On coding and engineering benchmarks it beat Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Fable 5 on several tests, though it trailed on some general reasoning benchmarks
Alibaba's Hong Kong and New York-listed shares jumped as much as **7%** on the announcement
Priced well below Western rivals at **$2** per million input tokens and **$6** per million output tokens, with a **1-million-token** context window
Full model weights will be open-sourced on Hugging Face and ModelScope **next week**, letting any developer download and run it

depth.background: Chinese tech giants have been racing to close the AI capability gap with US labs like Anthropic and OpenAI since ChatGPT's 2022 debut. Alibaba's Qwen family and Moonshot's Kimi K3, released just weeks earlier, represent the leading edge of that push, competing on both raw capability and price. **Mixture-of-experts** architecture — where a huge model only activates a fraction of its parameters per question — has become the industry's preferred way to build powerful yet affordable models. US export controls on advanced AI chips have pushed Chinese firms like Alibaba to squeeze more performance out of less computing power.

stories.title: England's Danni Wyatt-Hodge ruled out of the rest of The Hundred with a calf tear
stories.what_happened: Wyatt-Hodge picked up the injury while playing through discomfort during MI London's narrow loss to Southern Brave, where she still top-scored with an unbeaten **52**. Scans have since confirmed a **left calf tear**, ruling her out for the rest of the tournament. The Hundred has confirmed **Ella Claridge**, a 23-year-old batter who plays for the USA internationally and for The Blaze domestically, as her replacement in the MI London squad. The news follows fellow captain **Sophie Devine's** calf injury elsewhere in the competition, meaning two teams have lost key top-order batters to the same type of injury within days of each other. Wyatt-Hodge's 93 runs this season, at an average of 46.50, had made her one of the few bright spots in an otherwise winless campaign for MI London.
key_points: MI London's **Danni Wyatt-Hodge** ruled out of the remainder of the **Women's Hundred 2026** with a torn left calf.
The injury happened while she batted through pain for an unbeaten **52** against Southern Brave on July 27.
**Ella Claridge**, a 23-year-old USA international, has been signed as her replacement.
Wyatt-Hodge was MI London's joint-top run-scorer this season with **93 runs** at a strike rate of **132.85**.
MI London remain **winless** at the bottom of the table, now without one of their most in-form batters.

depth.background: The Hundred is England's short-format cricket competition where each team faces 100 balls per innings instead of the usual 120 in a T20. Danni Wyatt-Hodge is a veteran England international opening batter with over a decade of white-ball experience for her country. She plays for **MI London**, one of eight teams in the competition, who have struggled all season and sit **last** in the standings without a win. Losing an experienced international mid-season is a significant blow for a side already searching for answers.

stories.title: Lewis Hamilton welcomes new puppy Halo during F1's summer break
stories.what_happened: Hamilton has welcomed a golden retriever puppy named **Halo** into his home, sourced from US-based breeder Goldiva Goldens. It's his first dog since the loss of his beloved English bulldog **Roscoe**, who died of pneumonia last September at 13 years old. To help raise Halo, Hamilton hired **Kirstin McMillian**, a Los Angeles-based, three-generation animal trainer who previously worked with both Roscoe and his other dog, Coco. McMillian reportedly flew to Maine to begin preparing Halo before bringing her back to Los Angeles. The news went viral after Hamilton's partner, Kim Kardashian, posted the first photo of the puppy online, drawing heavy attention during F1's quiet summer break.
key_points: Hamilton has adopted a **golden retriever** puppy named Halo from US breeder Goldiva Goldens
It's his first dog since English bulldog **Roscoe** died of pneumonia last September at age **13**
Trainer **Kirstin McMillian**, who also worked with Roscoe, flew to Maine to prepare Halo before bringing her to Los Angeles
Partner **Kim Kardashian** shared the first public photo of Halo, sending the story viral
News broke during F1's mandatory **summer shutdown**, when the paddock and factories go quiet

depth.background: Hamilton, a seven-time world champion now driving for Ferrari, is known for his close bond with his pets, especially Roscoe, who traveled with him to races for years and became an unofficial F1 mascot before dying last September. Hamilton is dating media personality **Kim Kardashian**, and the couple's public life draws attention well beyond racing. F1's calendar includes a mandatory summer break after the Hungarian Grand Prix, when the paddock goes quiet and personal stories fill the news gap.

stories.title: Trump says US-Iran talks begin Monday to lock in a Hormuz deal — but Tehran denies any imminent session
stories.what_happened: Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday, Trump said the US had decided against delivering "a massive attack" on Iran after Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Iran itself asked Washington to hold off, with negotiations now set to begin **Monday afternoon**. Trump said the deal being discussed would include the **"Immediate, Complete, and Total"** reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, plus an end to Iran's nuclear weapons threat, and that he was setting no deadline for reaching it. However, Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson **Esmail Baghaei** told a press conference Monday that there is **no immediate plan** for negotiations with the US, reiterating that Tehran is currently only engaged in talks with **Oman** regarding the strait. The contradiction leaves it unclear whether the direct US-Iran session Trump described will actually happen today.
key_points: Trump says **US-Iran talks** begin Monday afternoon, with **no deadline** set for a deal.
The proposed deal covers a **'total' reopening of the Strait of Hormuz** and an end to Iran's nuclear program.
Trump says the US held off a **'massive attack'** at the request of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Iran itself.
Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson **Esmail Baghaei** denies any immediate plan for direct talks with the US.
Tehran says it is currently negotiating **only with Oman** over how ships cross the strait.

depth.background: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran for months, a conflict that escalated sharply in late July when Iran began targeting tankers to effectively choke off the **Strait of Hormuz** — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through daily. After ordering a new wave of strikes on July 31, Trump abruptly reversed course two days ago, citing an emerging deal brokered with help from Gulf states, but Iran never publicly confirmed the same terms Trump described.

thread.previously: We reported that Trump had paused a planned attack on Iran, saying 'the perimeters of a deal' to reopen the Strait of Hormuz had been reached with mediation from Qatar, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — though Iran had not publicly confirmed the same terms.
thread.changed: Trump now says direct US-Iran negotiations will begin Monday afternoon to nail down that deal, covering a full Hormuz reopening and an end to Iran's nuclear threat. But Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson says Tehran has no immediate plan for talks with Washington and is only negotiating with Oman over the strait — reviving doubt that a deal is actually close.

stories.title: Wall Street opens August bracing for Friday's jobs report as the biggest week of earnings season begins
stories.what_happened: US equity futures climbed Monday morning as investors kicked off August trading, with contracts tied to the **Dow Jones Industrial Average** up 265 points (0.9%), **S&P 500** futures up 0.55%, and **Nasdaq-100** futures up 0.93%. The day's first economic release is the **July ISM manufacturing index**, a widely watched gauge of US factory activity. **Palantir Technologies** reports earnings after the close today, kicking off a week that also includes **AMD, Eli Lilly and SanDisk**. The week's centerpiece is Friday's **July nonfarm payrolls report**, where economists polled by Dow Jones expect the economy added **87,500 jobs**, up from June's 57,000, while the unemployment rate is forecast to edge up to **4.3%** from 4.2%. So far this earnings season, roughly 300 S&P 500 companies have reported, and **85% have beaten analyst expectations**, according to FactSet.
key_points: US stock futures rose Monday, with Dow futures up **265 points (0.9%)** as August trading opened.
Friday brings the **July jobs report** — economists expect just **87,500 new jobs**, with unemployment ticking up to **4.3%**.
**Palantir** reports today, with **AMD, Eli Lilly and SanDisk** also headlining this week's earnings.
Of the roughly **300 S&P 500 companies** that have already reported, **85% beat expectations**.
Today's **ISM manufacturing index** — a survey of factory activity — is the first data point of the week.

depth.background: Each month, the US government's jobs report (officially the 'Employment Situation Summary') tells investors and the Federal Reserve how healthy the labor market really is — a weak number can mean the economy is slowing, while a too-strong one can worry the Fed about inflation. Coming into August, the second-quarter earnings season has been unusually strong, with the vast majority of large US companies beating Wall Street's profit forecasts. That combination — solid earnings, but a labor market that's expected to keep cooling — is what traders are weighing as the month opens.

stories.title: Oil prices drop as Trump's called-off Iran strike eases the war-risk premium baked into crude
stories.what_happened: Trading opened in Asia on Monday with oil prices falling hard: **WTI crude sank 4.5% to $80.89 a barrel**, and **Brent crude lost 4.4% to $84.10**. The move followed Trump's weekend statement that he had called off a planned strike on Iran, saying Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked the US to hold off because the outline of a deal had been agreed. With the immediate threat of a fresh military escalation reduced, traders unwound some of the extra risk premium they had built into crude prices over the previous two weeks. The pullback marks one of the largest single-day drops in oil this cycle, though prices remain well above where they stood before the crisis began.
key_points: US crude (WTI) fell **4.5%** to **$80.89 a barrel**; global benchmark Brent dropped **4.4%** to **$84.10**.
The drop came after Trump said he called off a planned strike on Iran, citing the outline of a deal.
Prices had surged as much as **24% in July alone** on fears of a wider war shutting the **Strait of Hormuz**.
About **one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil** normally passes through that single waterway.
Traders are betting the immediate escalation risk has passed, not that the underlying conflict is over.

depth.background: Oil prices had been climbing for weeks as the US and Israel traded strikes with Iran and tankers came under attack near the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow channel between Iran and Oman that carries a huge share of the world's crude. Every time a strike looked imminent, traders added a 'risk premium' to the price of oil — extra cost to cover the chance that supply gets disrupted, even if it never actually is. That premium pushed Brent up nearly a quarter in July alone, one of its sharpest monthly gains in years.

thread.previously: We reported Trump had called off a planned new wave of US strikes on Iran, saying Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for a pause while the outline of a deal came together.
thread.changed: That de-escalation is now showing up in hard numbers: oil traders spent the weekend pricing out some of the 'war premium' they had added to crude, and prices fell sharply in Monday trading.

stories.title: India's busiest earnings week of the quarter kicks off, with 350+ companies reporting through August 8
stories.what_happened: More than **350 companies on the BSE** are scheduled to report their April–June quarter (Q1 FY27) results between **August 3 and August 8**, making it one of the busiest stretches of the entire earnings season. Marquee names on the calendar include **State Bank of India, Bharti Airtel, ONGC, Power Grid, Marico, Titan Company, Hero MotoCorp, DLF, and Hindalco Industries**, spanning banking, telecom, energy, consumer goods, autos, and real estate. The results will be scrutinised for signs of whether India's economy — already the subject of debate ahead of this week's RBI rate decision — is growing as fast as recent GDP estimates suggest. Analysts will pay particular attention to bank earnings like SBI's for clues on loan growth and asset quality.
key_points: Over **350 listed Indian companies** report April–June (Q1 FY27) results between **August 3 and 8**.
Big names due this week include **SBI, Bharti Airtel, ONGC, Titan, and Hindalco**.
The week spans banking, telecom, energy, FMCG, pharma, autos and real estate.
Investors watch this window closely to gauge how the broader economy is holding up quarter to quarter.
State Bank of India, the country's largest lender, is among the marquee reports investors will parse for credit demand and bad-loan trends.

depth.background: Every quarter, thousands of Indian companies report their financial results in a compressed window, but the first week of August is traditionally one of the heaviest, catching a huge cross-section of the economy — banks, telecom operators, oil producers, consumer goods makers — all at once. Because India doesn't publish detailed monthly GDP data the way some countries do, these earnings reports are one of the clearest real-time signals investors and economists get on how businesses and consumers are actually doing.

stories.title: Parliament's Monsoon Session resumes today with the Supreme Court judges bill back on the table
stories.what_happened: Parliament's Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, having been adjourned amid continuing Opposition uproar, resume sitting today, August 3. On the agenda is the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026**, which would raise the court's sanctioned strength from 33 to 37 judges — a move meant to help the top court clear its backlog of pending cases faster. The bill formally replaces an ordinance the government had already used to make the same change on an interim basis. Whether it gets a substantive debate, or is rushed through like the births-and-deaths bill was, will be a live test of whether the session's gridlock has eased.
key_points: Both Houses of Parliament were adjourned until **today, August 3**, after days of Opposition disruption.
The Lok Sabha is due to take up the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026**.
The bill would raise the Supreme Court's sanctioned strength from **33 to 37 judges**.
It replaces an **earlier ordinance** the government had issued on the same subject.
Opposition protests have centred on a **police crackdown on a student march** over exam-related grievances.

depth.background: India's Monsoon Session of Parliament, running from mid-July to mid-August, has been repeatedly disrupted by Opposition protests over how police handled a student march earlier in the session. That disruption has meant several bills — including one on births-and-deaths registration — passed with little or no debate, which critics say undermines Parliament's basic job of scrutinising legislation. The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill was introduced by Law Minister **Arjun Ram Meghwal** to formally legislate an increase in judges that had previously been done through a temporary ordinance.

thread.previously: We reported the Lok Sabha had passed a births-and-deaths registration bill without debate as opposition uproar over a police crackdown on a student march paralysed proceedings, with both Houses eventually adjourned until August 3.
thread.changed: Parliament is back in session today, and the Lok Sabha is due to take up the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill — a chance to see whether the same disruption continues or business finally moves forward.

stories.title: Beth Mooney powers Trent Rockets Women past Welsh Fire in Cardiff for a second Hundred win
stories.what_happened: At Cardiff, **Trent Rockets Women** chased down Welsh Fire Women's total of **129 for 3** with 17 balls to spare, winning by 8 wickets. **Beth Mooney** led the chase with a rapid 57 off 35 balls, laying the foundation before **Nat Sciver-Brunt (37 not out off 23 balls)** and **Ash Gardner (10 not out off 9 balls)** finished the job together at the crease. The win was Trent Rockets Women's second of the season, marking a positive turn in form after an inconsistent start to their Hundred campaign.
key_points: Trent Rockets Women beat Welsh Fire Women by **8 wickets** in Cardiff.
**Beth Mooney** top-scored with **57 off 35 balls**, setting up the chase.
Welsh Fire were restricted to **129 for 3** from their 100 balls.
Trent Rockets chased the target down with **17 balls to spare**.
**Nat Sciver-Brunt (37 not out)** and **Ash Gardner (10 not out)** finished the innings together.

depth.background: The Hundred is England's short-format cricket competition, played over 100 balls per side rather than the more familiar 20-over T20 format, and features both men's and women's franchise teams competing in parallel tournaments each summer. Welsh Fire Women had been in strong form this season, making this result a notable upset for Trent Rockets Women, who picked up just their second win of the competition.

stories.title: Israel's Gaza strikes kill 17 in the deadliest day in weeks, even as a US-brokered disarmament plan is supposed to be taking hold
stories.what_happened: Israeli forces carried out strikes across multiple Gaza locations on August 3, killing at least **17 Palestinians** — the deadliest single day in the enclave in several weeks, according to Palestinian health officials. In Deir al-Balah, an air raid killed a married couple, 68-year-old Kamal Abu Muailiq and his 59-year-old wife Huda. In Gaza City's Remal neighbourhood, a drone strike hit a tent sheltering displaced people, killing two, including a child. Separately, four people were killed when a strike hit a vehicle in Gaza City, and a person was directly targeted and killed in the Jabalia refugee camp in the north. **Nickolay Mladenov**, the Board of Peace's Gaza envoy, said the past two days of strikes had killed civilians and destroyed medical supplies people depend on.
key_points: **17 Palestinians killed** across Gaza on August 3 — the highest single-day toll in weeks.
An elderly couple, **Kamal and Huda Abu Muailiq**, died in an air raid on their home in Deir al-Balah.
A child was among two people killed in a **drone strike on a displaced-persons tent** in Gaza City's Remal area.
The strikes come despite Hamas reportedly agreeing to **disarm** under a US-drafted peace framework.
The UN-linked Gaza peace envoy says the strikes have **destroyed medical supplies** civilians depend on.

depth.background: In late July, US President **Donald Trump** announced Hamas had agreed to hand over its weapons as part of a broader plan to end the two-year Gaza war. That plan also calls for Israel to gradually **withdraw from Gaza** and transfer administrative power to a Palestinian authority — terms Israeli politicians and much of the Israeli press have received coolly. Two days ago we reported Israeli strikes had already killed nine people despite the supposed disarmament breakthrough, with a senior Israeli minister flatly denying any deal existed to stop the attacks. The gap between the diplomatic announcement in Washington and the reality on the ground in Gaza has only widened since.

thread.previously: We reported that Israeli strikes had killed nine people in Gaza for a second straight day, with an Israeli minister publicly denying any deal was in place to stop the attacks, even as Hamas had reportedly agreed to disarm under a US-backed plan.
thread.changed: The death toll jumped sharply: at least **17 Palestinians were killed** on August 3, the worst single day in weeks, including a married couple in their 60s and a child, showing the 'no deal to stop attacks' stance from two days ago has held even as the wider disarmament plan is meant to be moving forward.

stories.title: RBI's rate-setting committee begins its 3-day meeting today, with markets betting on a hold at 5.25%
stories.what_happened: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee began its three-day rate-setting meeting today, August 3, with Governor Sanjay Malhotra due to announce the decision on August 5. A Reuters survey of 72 economists found overwhelming consensus for a hold: 68 expect the repo rate to remain unchanged at **5.25%**, four expect a 25-basis-point hike, and none expect a cut. The committee is weighing elevated crude oil prices — worsened by the ongoing Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions — and monsoon-driven food-price risk against recent strong growth data, with SBI Research raising its Q1 growth estimate to roughly 7% just a day before the meeting began.
key_points: The RBI's **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** meets August 3–5; Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** announces the decision on August 5.
A Reuters poll of 72 economists found **68 expect the repo rate to stay at 5.25%**, only 4 expect a hike, none expect a cut.
The repo rate was last cut by **25 basis points to 5.25%** in December 2025.
The committee is balancing **rising inflation risk** from Gulf oil prices and an uneven monsoon against **strong growth** — SBI Research just raised its Q1 growth estimate to around 7%.
Expect the RBI to keep its policy stance **'neutral'** but strike a more hawkish tone in its commentary.

depth.background: India's central bank, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, sets the country's benchmark interest rate — the **repo rate**, the rate at which it lends to commercial banks — through a six-member Monetary Policy Committee that meets roughly every two months. The RBI's job is to balance keeping inflation in check with supporting economic growth; it cut rates in December 2025 to help growth, and has held steady since. This meeting lands at an unusually complicated moment: the Strait of Hormuz crisis (see our linked story) has kept crude oil prices elevated for months, directly feeding into India's import bill and inflation, while heavy monsoon flooding in Assam, Kerala, and Gujarat adds further uncertainty to food prices and growth.

stories.title: Mumbai Indians publicly deny CSK trade talks over Hardik Pandya, calling reports 'contrary' to fact
stories.what_happened: A Mumbai Indians spokesperson pushed back directly on days of trade speculation, saying: 'Contrary to reports, we are not engaged in conversations regarding player trades; any trade would only be possible once the review is complete.' This contradicts specific reports from earlier this week claiming MI wanted CSK's Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre in exchange for handing over Pandya, with CSK reportedly offering Dube, Dewald Brevis, and roughly ₹10 crore in cash as an alternative package. The speculation had been fueled by Pandya's weak IPL 2026 numbers — just 206 runs at an average of 22.89 with no half-centuries, and an economy rate of 11.43 with the ball — alongside Mumbai Indians' failure to make the playoffs.
key_points: A Mumbai Indians spokesperson said: **'we are not engaged in conversations regarding player trades.'**
MI says any trade decision can only happen **after its post-season review is complete**.
Reports had claimed MI wanted **Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre** from CSK in exchange for Hardik Pandya.
Pandya's IPL 2026 season was poor: **206 runs at 22.89**, no fifties, and an economy rate of 11.43 with the ball.
Mumbai Indians **missed the IPL 2026 playoffs**, fueling scrutiny of Pandya's captaincy.

depth.background: Hardik Pandya has captained Mumbai Indians since returning to the franchise in 2024, but the team has struggled since, missing the IPL 2026 playoffs entirely — a poor result that has put his captaincy and place in the squad under public scrutiny. Speculation about a trade to Chennai Super Kings (CSK), the franchise he started his career away from, built through late July and into this week, with multiple reports naming specific players CSK might offer in exchange, even though neither franchise had confirmed anything officially.

thread.previously: We reported that Chennai Super Kings had joined the race for Hardik Pandya, with reports saying up to seven IPL franchises now wanted him, and that CSK were reportedly prepared to offer cash plus a player swap.
thread.changed: Mumbai Indians has now **officially denied** being in trade talks with CSK or anyone else, saying its post-season review isn't even finished yet — directly contradicting the specific swap terms (Shivam Dube, Ayush Mhatre, and cash) that had been widely reported.
