stories.title: Bangladesh get a big boost as wicketkeeper Litton Das returns to the squad for their historic Australia Test tour
stories.what_happened: The **Bangladesh Cricket Board** announced on **Saturday, August 1**, that **Litton Das** has been added to the squad for the opening Test against Australia in Darwin, after showing encouraging progress recovering from a **calf injury** he suffered during the third ODI against Australia at home on **June 14**. His return significantly strengthens a squad that had been announced as **pace-depleted** just days earlier — with lead strike bowler **Nahid Rana** ruled out by a side strain and left-arm seamer **Shoriful Islam** missing out through a hamstring injury, and uncapped fast bowler **Musfik Hasan** getting a first call-up as pace cover. Litton is scheduled to join the squad in Australia as preparations intensify for the **August 13** series opener in Darwin — a tour that marks Bangladesh's first-ever Test appearances on Australian soil.
key_points: **Litton Das**, Bangladesh's experienced wicketkeeper-batter, has been **added back** to the squad for the first Test against Australia.
He'd been out with a **calf injury** sustained during the third ODI against Australia at home on **June 14**.
The Bangladesh Cricket Board confirmed his inclusion on **Saturday, August 1**, citing encouraging progress in rehab.
The first Test starts in **Darwin on August 13** — Bangladesh's **first-ever Test appearance in Australia**.
The squad remains **pace-depleted**: strike bowler **Nahid Rana** is out with a side strain, and **Shoriful Islam** misses out with a hamstring injury.

depth.background: Bangladesh named their squad for this historic two-Test tour of Australia (Darwin August 13–17, Mackay August 22–26) last week, but it was a squad short on fast-bowling firepower and, notably, without a single player who'd previously played a Test in Australian conditions — a tough ask against a team that dominates at home. Litton Das is one of Bangladesh's most experienced white-ball and red-ball wicketkeeper-batters, and his absence would have been a significant loss of both batting depth and glovework experience for a squad already facing a steep challenge.

thread.previously: We reported Bangladesh named a 15-member squad for their historic Australia tour that was short on fast bowlers, with uncapped Musfik Hasan getting a first call-up after injuries ruled out Nahid Rana, and no player in the squad with prior Test experience in Australia.
thread.changed: Litton Das has now been added back to the squad after recovering from a calf injury, restoring experienced batting and wicketkeeping depth even as the pace-bowling shortage remains unresolved.

stories.title: Mumbai Indians shut the door on Hardik Pandya trade talks with CSK, as the saga stalls
stories.what_happened: **Mumbai Indians** have reportedly stepped back from active trade discussions with **Chennai Super Kings** over their captain **Hardik Pandya**, effectively shutting down that particular negotiating track — at least for now. The deal had stalled over MI's insistence on receiving **both Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre** in any swap, a package CSK were not willing to offer given how highly they rate Mhatre. Mumbai's official spokesperson has publicly **denied** that Pandya is being actively shopped to any franchise, pushing back on the wave of trade reports that had built up over recent days. That denial sits alongside continuing reports of separate interest from **Delhi Capitals, Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals**, none of which have been confirmed. As of now, **no trade involving Pandya has been finalized**, and his status for the coming IPL season remains an open question.
key_points: **Mumbai Indians** have reportedly pulled back from active negotiations with **Chennai Super Kings (CSK)** over a Hardik Pandya trade, with no deal currently being pursued.
The sticking point had been MI's demand for **both Shivam Dube and young opener Ayush Mhatre** in exchange for their captain — CSK were unwilling to part with Mhatre.
MI's official line: they have **denied** reports that Pandya is being actively shopped, even as talks with multiple franchises had been ongoing.
**Delhi Capitals, Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals** had all separately been reported as interested parties before this pullback.
As things stand, **no trade has been completed** and Pandya's franchise future for the next season remains unresolved.

depth.background: **Hardik Pandya**, Mumbai Indians' captain and one of Indian cricket's premier all-rounders, has been at the center of an escalating trade saga this off-season, with multiple IPL franchises reportedly circling. CSK had proposed swapping all-rounder **Shivam Dube** for Pandya, while MI countered by asking for Dube plus rising opener **Ayush Mhatre** — a demand CSK were unwilling to meet given Mhatre's rising value. Delhi Capitals had separately floated a package built around Axar Patel and Prithvi Shaw (or Sameer Rizvi), while Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals had also made informal contact with MI. None of these discussions had been officially confirmed by any franchise before this latest development.

stories.title: Max Verstappen's Red Bull exit clause is now active — and a pundit says his radio rants at Hungary looked like he's angling for the door
stories.what_happened: Verstappen went into Formula 1's summer break well outside the top of the drivers' championship, which — according to German outlet **BILD** — automatically **triggered the performance clause** in his Red Bull contract, giving him a formal window to decide whether to leave the team before his deal expires in 2028. During the Hungarian Grand Prix weekend, Verstappen's frustrated in-race radio messages about the car's handling drew attention, and Sky Sports commentator **David Croft** said on **August 1** that he suspected Verstappen and his management were **'trying to engineer a way out of Red Bull and maybe into McLaren.'** Red Bull has responded by tabling a new contract offer that would extend Verstappen's stay through **2029** at roughly **$80 million per season**, on condition that the exit clause is scrapped. Verstappen's camp has not yet formally responded to the offer. Former F1 driver **Robert Doornbos** has suggested Verstappen could confirm his decision at the **Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort** later this month, though the contractual deadline to decide runs to **October**.
key_points: Verstappen's Red Bull contract has a **performance-based exit clause** tied to his championship position at the summer break.
He finished the Hungarian Grand Prix weekend **outside the top two/three** in the standings, which **activated the clause**, per BILD.
Sky Sports' **David Croft** suggested Verstappen and his camp may be **'trying to engineer a way out'** of Red Bull, possibly to McLaren.
Red Bull has offered Verstappen a new deal through **2029**, reportedly worth roughly **$80 million a season**, that would **remove the clause** entirely.
Verstappen has **until October** to decide whether to invoke the clause and leave, with an announcement possibly expected at the **Dutch Grand Prix** in Zandvoort.

depth.background: Verstappen signed his current Red Bull contract, running through **2028**, at the peak of his dominance, but it included an unusual **opt-out clause**: if he wasn't running near the front of the championship by the summer break, he could walk away early. Red Bull's car has struggled to match Mercedes and McLaren for pace this season, and Verstappen has openly vented frustration over team radio during races, including calling his car **'horrendous'** and **'undrivable'** during the Hungarian Grand Prix weekend.

stories.title: Modi inaugurates a new international airport and semiconductor plant in a ₹18,000 crore Andhra Pradesh push
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Andhra Pradesh on **Saturday, August 1**, and inaugurated or laid foundation stones for projects worth close to **₹18,000 crore (about $2.1 billion)**. The headline project is the new **Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport** at Bhogapuram in Vizianagaram district, built as a public-private partnership at a cost of over **₹5,640 crore**, designed to handle **6 million passengers a year**, roughly 45 km from Visakhapatnam. Modi also laid the foundation stone for a **₹460 crore semiconductor project** in Visakhapatnam, being built by ASIP Technologies with South Korea's **APACT**. Other projects included transmission infrastructure for the Kurnool Wind and Solar Energy Zone worth about ₹3,550 crore, and a POWERGRID transmission scheme serving 2,500 MW of solar capacity in Ananthapuram and 1,000 MW in Kurnool, worth over ₹820 crore. AP Chief Minister **N. Chandrababu Naidu** and Deputy CM **Pawan Kalyan** attended alongside Modi.
key_points: Modi inaugurated projects worth nearly **₹18,000 crore ($2.1 billion)** in Andhra Pradesh.
The centerpiece: the new **Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport** at Bhogapuram, built for **6 million passengers a year**.
He laid the foundation for a **₹460 crore semiconductor plant** with South Korea's APACT.
Also included: over **₹4,370 crore** in transmission infrastructure for wind and solar energy zones.
AP's coalition government — a key national NDA ally — hosted the visit.

depth.background: Andhra Pradesh's government, led by Chief Minister **N. Chandrababu Naidu**'s Telugu Desam Party in coalition with **Pawan Kalyan**'s Jana Sena, is a significant ally of the BJP-led coalition at the national level, and big central infrastructure investment there reflects that political relationship. The new airport is named after **Alluri Sitarama Raju**, a tribal freedom fighter who led an armed uprising against British colonial rule in the 1920s. The semiconductor project connects to India's broader 'Make in India' push to build domestic chip-manufacturing capacity, part of a global race — especially amid US-China tech tensions — to reduce reliance on the small handful of countries, mainly Taiwan, that dominate advanced chip production today.

stories.title: Ellyse Perry's unbeaten 68 drags Birmingham Phoenix Women to their first win of the season, beating Welsh Fire with a ball to spare
stories.what_happened: Playing at **Edgbaston** in Birmingham on August 1, Welsh Fire posted **144 for 3**, built on Georgia Voll's **78 off 55 balls**, who started slowly through the powerplay before accelerating hard against the spinners and bringing up her half-century with a six. Chasing 145, Birmingham Phoenix lost early momentum before **Perry and Alice Capsey** came together and added **86 runs for the third wicket**, with Capsey striking 51 off just 29 balls. Capsey had also taken two wickets earlier in the Welsh Fire innings, making it a strong all-round game for her. Perry finished the job herself, hitting Welsh Fire bowler Heather Graham for **10 runs in two balls** at the death to get Phoenix home with just one ball remaining, sealing a **seven-wicket win** and her side's first victory of the season.
key_points: Birmingham Phoenix Women chased down Welsh Fire's 144/3 to win by **7 wickets**, getting there with just **one ball to spare**.
Australian veteran **Ellyse Perry** anchored the chase, finishing unbeaten on **68 off 46 balls** and was named Player of the Match.
Perry and **Alice Capsey** (51 off 29) put on an **86-run stand** that turned a stuttering chase into a win.
Welsh Fire's total was built around a blazing **78 from 22-year-old Georgia Voll**, one of Australia's fastest-rising batters.
The win is Phoenix's **first of the 2026 Hundred season**, ending a winless start to their campaign.

depth.background: **The Hundred** is England and Wales' short-format franchise cricket competition, launched by the ECB in 2021 to bring new, younger and more casual fans to the sport. Each side faces **100 balls per innings** (instead of the 120 balls of a normal T20), split into blocks of five or ten, which speeds up the game and gives bowlers a slightly different tactical puzzle. Birmingham Phoenix Women had gone the opening weeks of this season without a win, while **Ellyse Perry** — regarded as one of the greatest all-rounders the women's game has produced, and Australia's youngest-ever senior international when she debuted in 2007 — was signed specifically to add experience and finishing power to their top order. Welsh Fire, meanwhile, had been leaning on Voll, a young Australian batter who broke into her national side only in the last year and has quickly become one of the most sought-after overseas signings in franchise cricket.

stories.title: Esteban Ocon's Haas seat is in real jeopardy for 2027 as three replacements circle
stories.what_happened: With his Haas contract running out at the end of the year, Ocon's position for **2027** has come under growing scrutiny after a difficult season: he has managed just **3 points** through the first 10 rounds, while rookie teammate **Oliver Bearman** has already built a **15-point** lead over him. Haas is reported to be actively weighing replacements, with three names in the frame — **Leonardo Fornaroli**, McLaren's reserve driver; **Rafael Câmara**, a Ferrari junior driver; and **Yuki Tsunoda**, who lost his Red Bull seat earlier this year. Haas holds a contractual option to extend Ocon for a third season but is reportedly in no rush to exercise it, with the broader 2027 driver market still unsettled. Bearman, notably, also isn't yet contracted to Haas beyond 2026, though he's considered likely to stay unless a seat opens up at Ferrari itself. Asked about his own future, Ocon said simply he has **'nothing to announce.'**
key_points: Ocon has scored just **3 points across the first 10 rounds** of 2026, while rookie teammate **Oliver Bearman is already 15 points clear**.
Ocon's Haas contract **expires at the end of 2026**, and the team holds an option to extend him for a third year but isn't rushing to use it.
Three names have emerged as candidates to replace him: **Leonardo Fornaroli** (McLaren reserve), **Rafael Câmara** (Ferrari junior), and **Yuki Tsunoda** (former Red Bull driver).
**Bearman himself isn't contracted to Haas for 2027**, but is considered likely to stay barring a Ferrari seat opening up.
Ocon told reporters he has **'nothing to announce'** on his own future.

depth.background: Ocon joined Haas for 2025 after a rocky final season at Alpine, pairing with rookie Oliver Bearman for 2026. Haas has generally been a midfield team competing for minor points, and a driver's seat there hinges on outscoring — or at least keeping pace with — the teammate, since results are the team's clearest currency for sponsorship and prize money.

stories.title: Alex Albon says Williams' hoped-for title challenge is now years further away than planned
stories.what_happened: Alex Albon said Williams' rebuild is now running well behind where he expected, telling reporters **'it definitely feels like we've taken two or three years back'** compared to the timeline he had in mind. He had previously hoped 2027 could bring consistent podiums and occasional race wins; that expectation has now shifted. Williams struggled from the start of 2026, skipping a scheduled shakedown test in Barcelona and arriving at the season-opening Bahrain test with a car that was **significantly overweight**. Despite Vowles' overhaul of the team's people and processes, Albon said the new regulations have exposed **bigger structural issues** than anticipated. The team has scored just 11 points this season and sits ninth in the constructors' standings.
key_points: Albon says Williams has **'taken two or three years back'** on its recovery timeline
He'd once hoped for **podiums and wins by 2027** — that's no longer realistic
Williams has scored just **11 points** this season, ninth in the constructors' championship
The team **skipped pre-season testing** in Barcelona and arrived overweight in Bahrain
New rules meant to help Williams have instead **exposed deeper structural problems**

depth.background: Williams is one of F1's oldest and most storied teams, but spent years near the back of the grid before principal **James Vowles** took over in 2023 with a multi-year rebuilding plan. 2026 brought a **major regulation reset** — new engine and chassis rules across F1 — which smaller teams like Williams had hoped would let them close the gap to the big-budget teams, since everyone effectively started from scratch on car design.

stories.title: Israeli strikes kill seven across Gaza and destroy a hospital's medicine stockpile as the 'Board of Peace' spells out how Hamas must actually disarm
stories.what_happened: Israeli forces carried out several strikes across Gaza on **Saturday, August 1**, killing at least **seven Palestinians** — a man and his wife in an apartment strike in Deir al-Balah, two more people including a child in a separate strike on a Gaza City apartment, and others in additional attacks. Separately, strikes destroyed **medicine storage warehouses** located beside a hospital, further damaging Gaza's medical supply chain. On the diplomatic track, the Board of Peace — the oversight body set up under Trump's plan — detailed for the first time exactly how Hamas's weapons are meant to leave circulation: heavy weapons, production sites, depots and the tunnel network are targeted first, inventoried and stored by a new **Palestinian National Committee** whose police officers must individually clear **Shin Bet security vetting**. No weapons are to be handed to Israel or any non-Palestinian party. An **international verification commission** and the **International Stabilization Force** will monitor the process, with Israeli troops withdrawing from designated lines only as disarmament is verified — not on a preset timetable.
key_points: Israeli strikes on **Saturday** killed at least **seven Palestinians** across Gaza, including a married couple in Deir al-Balah and a child in Gaza City.
Separate strikes destroyed **medicine storage warehouses** next to a hospital, hitting the territory's already-crippled healthcare supply.
The **Board of Peace** — the US-backed panel overseeing Trump's peace plan — released the first real blueprint for Hamas's disarmament: weapons go into **Palestinian-run storage**, not to Israel.
Storage-site police must pass **Shin Bet (Israeli intelligence) vetting**, with an **International Stabilization Force** providing outside oversight.
Israeli troops are set to withdraw only **incrementally, tied to verified disarmament progress** — not on a fixed date.

depth.background: Hamas signed a 15-point disarmament framework on **July 31**, the biggest step yet in the US-brokered push to end the Gaza war after nearly two years of fighting. Israel didn't reject the deal outright but said its core demand — **full demilitarization** — hadn't been met, and strikes have continued through the supposed **two-week ceasefire window** meant to work out implementation. Since the ceasefire technically began in **October 2025**, Israeli strikes have killed more than **1,200 Palestinians**, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, on top of an overall death toll above **73,000** since the war began in 2023.

thread.previously: We reported Hamas had just signed a 15-point disarmament framework and Israel responded with strikes rather than confirmation, killing at least two Palestinians, with a two-week window nominally in place to work out implementation.
thread.changed: The death toll from continued strikes has risen sharply (seven killed Saturday, including a destroyed medicine warehouse), and the Board of Peace has now published the actual mechanics of how Hamas's disarmament is supposed to work — Palestinian-run, Shin Bet-vetted storage sites overseen by an international force.

stories.title: Joe Root says new coach Stephen Fleming was a 'big reason' he agreed to take England's Test captaincy back
stories.what_happened: Speaking after the ECB confirmed the new coaching and captaincy setup, **Joe Root** said that **Stephen Fleming's** appointment as England's Test head coach was a **'big reason'** he agreed to return as captain. Root said: **'We've spoken briefly and if I'm being brutally honest he was a big reason why I wanted to do it. I'm very excited by the way he sees the game, where he sees us sit as a team and the work we have to do to get to where we want to get to.'** The 35-year-old Root returns to the captaincy for the first time since his 2022 resignation, taking over from Ben Stokes, while Fleming replaces Brendon McCullum as head coach. Root's first assignment in the role will be a **three-Test home series against Pakistan starting August 19**, with Fleming's first assignment continuing into England's winter tour of South Africa.
key_points: **Joe Root** is back as England's **Test captain**, four years after stepping down from the role.
New head coach **Stephen Fleming** was, in Root's own words, a **'big reason'** he wanted the job again.
The pair succeed **Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes**, who stepped down as coach and captain respectively.
Root called himself **'very excited'** by how Fleming sees the game and where England needs to get to.
Root's first assignment is a **three-Test home series against Pakistan**.

depth.background: Joe Root is England's all-time leading Test run-scorer and previously captained the side for a record 64 matches between 2017 and 2022, before stepping down under pressure after a difficult run of results. Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes then took England's Test side in a famously attacking direction, but both have now moved on from their respective coaching and captaincy roles, prompting the ECB to turn back to Root and bring in New Zealand great **Stephen Fleming** — previously head coach of IPL side Chennai Super Kings — as the new Test head coach.

stories.title: Preeti Pawar wins India's first Commonwealth Games boxing gold as 10 Indian boxers reach the finals in Glasgow
stories.what_happened: On Day 9 of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games (Saturday, August 1), India's Preeti Pawar defeated Canada's Scarlett Savannah Delgado by a **5-0** judges' decision to win gold — one of **10 gold-medal boxing bouts** India contested on the day, an unprecedented number for a single Games. Jaismine Lamboria also won her first round on the way to her own final against Michaela Walsh of Northern Ireland. The boxing finals followed a big day for India across combat sports: judokas Asmita Dey and Harsh Singh won India's first-ever Commonwealth judo gold medals on Friday, with more Indian judokas still competing in later rounds. Track star Gulveer Singh was also due to run the men's 5000m final, looking to add to the 10,000m silver he'd already won.
key_points: India's **Preeti Pawar beat Canada's Scarlett Savannah Delgado 5-0** to win India's first boxing gold medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.
An unprecedented **10 Indian boxers reached the gold-medal finals** in Glasgow — the country's biggest-ever Commonwealth boxing campaign, guaranteeing at least **10 silver medals**.
Olympic medallist **Lovlina Borgohain** leads the group chasing gold on what's being called India's biggest day yet at these Games.
It comes a day after India's judokas — **Asmita Dey and Harsh Singh** — won the country's first-ever Commonwealth Games judo golds.
India currently sits **10th in the medal tally** with 23 medals (5 gold, 12 silver, 6 bronze) heading into Saturday's events.

depth.background: The Commonwealth Games bring together athletes from roughly 56 countries and territories of the Commonwealth (mostly former British Empire nations) every four years. India has traditionally been strongest at these Games in boxing, wrestling, weightlifting, and badminton — sports where it's historically punched below its weight at the larger Olympics. The 2026 Games are being held in Glasgow, Scotland, and this edition has already been a breakout one for Indian boxing and judo.

stories.title: Zelensky says Ukraine's air defenses are being 'overwhelmed' as Russia launches a second massive strike in two days
stories.what_happened: Russia launched a second massive aerial assault on Ukraine within 48 hours, this time striking Kyiv and surrounding regions with a wave of **ballistic missiles and drones**. Ukrainian officials said **9 people were killed and 30 wounded**, including four children. Critically, Ukraine's military reported it managed to shoot down only **one of the 27 ballistic missiles** Russia fired — a strikingly low interception rate that officials attribute directly to a **shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles**. President Zelensky said on Telegram that the shortfall in anti-ballistic interceptors is now actively encouraging Russia to keep launching these strikes, since it knows they will largely get through. The attack extended as far west as **Lviv**, near the Polish border, prompting **Poland** to scramble its own fighter jets as a precaution. Zelensky renewed his appeal to Western allies for more Patriot interceptors, warning that the current pace of Russian strikes is outstripping what Ukraine can currently intercept.
key_points: Russia hit Ukraine with another huge missile-and-drone barrage — the **second major assault in 48 hours** — killing **9 people and wounding 30**, including **4 children**.
Only **1 of 27 ballistic missiles** launched was shot down, exposing a severe gap in Ukraine's ability to intercept Russia's most advanced weapons.
President **Zelensky** says Ukraine is critically short of **interceptor missiles for its US-made Patriot air-defense systems** — the only system that can reliably down ballistic missiles.
Russia appears to be deliberately testing and exposing Kyiv's weakened air defenses as its ground offensive struggles to advance along the front line.
Strikes have reached as far west as **Lviv**, forcing NATO member **Poland** to scramble fighter jets to secure its own airspace.

depth.background: Ukraine's air-defense network relies heavily on Western-supplied systems, and **Patriot batteries** are the only ones capable of reliably intercepting Russia's fast, high-flying **ballistic missiles** (as opposed to slower cruise missiles or drones, which other systems can handle). Deliveries of Patriot interceptors depend on the US and European allies, and have repeatedly lagged behind what Ukraine says it needs, especially as US political support has grown more uncertain. Russia has increasingly timed massive combined missile-and-drone barrages to arrive back-to-back, aiming to exhaust both Ukraine's defenses and its stockpile of interceptors faster than they can be resupplied.

thread.previously: We reported Russia's heaviest barrage on Kyiv in weeks killed at least 9 people and wounded 27, with Zelensky pressing allies for more Patriot interceptors after Ukraine struck back at a Russian oil refinery.
thread.changed: A second massive barrage hit just a day later, and this time Ukraine could only intercept 1 of 27 ballistic missiles fired — Zelensky is now explicitly warning that the Patriot interceptor shortage is a critical vulnerability Russia is exploiting.

stories.title: F1 reopens talks with Hockenheim over a long-term German Grand Prix return
stories.what_happened: Domenicali revealed in a wide-ranging interview that **'we are reconnected with the possibility of having contact with the Hockenheim people'** about a future race, stressing this is about a **long-term**, not short-term, return. He linked the renewed interest partly to F1's changing media landscape in Germany: a deal with broadcaster **RTL**, and, for the first time, more than one operator competing for German broadcast rights, which he said shows Europe's importance to F1 is 'getting even bigger.' Hockenheimring managing director **Jorn Teske** confirmed talks are happening but played down suggestions a deal is close, saying **'there is interest, but at this time we have no results to report,'** and that the track wants an economically viable arrangement.
key_points: F1 boss **Stefano Domenicali** says Hockenheim reached out first about a comeback
Germany has been **off the F1 calendar since 2019** (its last race was won by Verstappen)
Any deal would be **long-term, not a quick fix** — talks are still very early
A new **media rights deal with RTL** and rising broadcaster interest is one driver
Hockenheim's own boss says there's **'no results to report'** yet

depth.background: Germany was once a fixture on the Formula 1 calendar, with races held at Hockenheim and the Nurburgring for decades — home to legends like Michael Schumacher. But the German Grand Prix fell off the calendar after **2019** as F1 expanded into newer markets like Miami, Las Vegas and Saudi Arabia, and Hockenheim struggled to make the economics of hosting a race work without government subsidy. F1 has spent recent seasons prioritizing races that can pay large hosting fees, while trying to keep its European 'heartland' races relevant.

stories.title: Fernando Alonso says he'll decide his F1 future during the summer break — and shoots down Alpine return talk
stories.what_happened: Alonso confirmed he plans to make a decision on his **2027 F1 future during the summer break**, which began after the Hungarian Grand Prix, with an announcement likely to land around the Zandvoort or Monza race weekends later in August/September. He was explicit that the timing and scale of Aston Martin's long-awaited car upgrade — finally introduced at the Hungarian Grand Prix — will **not** be the deciding factor; instead, he says the deciding question is whether he still enjoys racing under F1's new regulations. Alonso reaffirmed his commitment to Aston Martin 'beyond his driving time,' pushing back on speculation he could jump to Alpine and replace young driver **Franco Colapinto**, which paddock insiders say should be dismissed as rumour. Colapinto himself said this week that Aston Martin has become noticeably faster than Alpine in corners since the upgrade landed.
key_points: Alonso, F1's oldest driver at **45**, says he'll decide on racing in **2027** during the August break.
He insists the call depends on **F1's regulations and how much he still enjoys driving** — not Aston Martin's car upgrades.
Speculation that he'd **replace Franco Colapinto at Alpine** should be dismissed as 'paddock speculation,' per insiders.
Aston Martin's big upgrade finally arrived at the **Hungarian Grand Prix** after a difficult first half of the season.
Alonso says his commitment to Aston Martin **goes beyond his driving time** despite the team's season-long struggles.

depth.background: Fernando Alonso is a two-time world champion and, at 45, the oldest driver on the current F1 grid, now in his third stint with Aston Martin (formerly Renault, then McLaren, then Alpine, now Aston Martin) chasing an elusive third title. Aston Martin has struggled through the first half of the new-regulation 2026 season, prompting persistent speculation about whether Alonso would retire, or move to a stronger team — including rumours of a return to Alpine, the team he won both his championships with in 2005-06. F1's new car and engine rules for 2026 have reshuffled the competitive order, which matters a lot to a driver in his final career seasons deciding whether the sport is still worth it.

stories.title: A dead SpaceX rocket stage is about to crash into the Moon at 5,400 mph
stories.what_happened: The spent Falcon 9 upper stage is projected to strike the Moon on **Wednesday, August 5, at roughly 2:34 a.m. ET**, hitting the surface at about **5,400 mph** — seven times the speed of sound. Space-tracking expert Bill Gray calculates the impact point will be near **Einstein Crater**, on the Moon's sunlit, Earth-facing side. The collision is expected to gouge out a fresh crater roughly **16 feet deep and 89 feet across**, and could throw up a multi-kilometer plume of dust visible through amateur telescopes from the eastern US, Canada, and much of South America. A team of planetary scientists is coordinating a public campaign asking astronomers to watch and record the impact, since an object of known mass and speed hitting a known spot offers a rare, precisely-measured data point for studying the Moon's subsurface. SpaceX has since improved its practices for newer missions, steering at least one more recent upper stage into a long-term solar orbit instead of leaving it adrift.
key_points: The Falcon 9 upper stage will slam into the Moon on **August 5** near Einstein Crater, moving at **5,400 mph**
It's the leftover stage from a **January 2025** launch that carried two lunar landers and drifted for 19 months
Scientists expect it to carve a crater roughly **16 feet deep and 89 feet wide**
The crash was **never planned** — a nudge into solar orbit could have avoided it
Astronomers across the **eastern US, Canada and South America** may spot the debris plume through a telescope

depth.background: SpaceX regularly sends its Falcon 9 rocket's upper stage into deep space on missions bound for the Moon or beyond, and once the stage releases its payload it becomes space junk with no further use. On January 15, 2025, one such stage helped launch two private Moon landers — Firefly Aerospace's **Blue Ghost** and ispace's **Resilience** — toward the Moon. Because no rule required a safe disposal plan for the leftover stage, it was left drifting through space, slowly pulled off course by the gravity of Earth, the Moon and the Sun. Nineteen months later, that drift has put it on a direct collision course with the lunar surface.

stories.title: Trump asks the Supreme Court to revive his mail-voting crackdown — and his own party's governors are pushing back
stories.what_happened: A federal judge ruled last month that it's unconstitutional for the federal government to dictate how states administer their elections, blocking Trump's order in the affected states. On **July 27**, the Trump administration asked the **Supreme Court** to lift that block and let the order take effect while the broader legal fight continues. In response, **Vermont's Republican governor Phil Scott** publicly defended his state's mail-in voting system and rejected Trump's call for Republicans to 'nationalize' elections. Arizona's Secretary of State, **Adrian Fontes**, went further, calling the order unconstitutional and noting that mail-in ballots were designed by Republicans in his state and have actually helped keep the GOP competitive there for years. The pushback shows the fight isn't purely partisan — some Republican officials are siding with Democrats against the White House on this one.
key_points: Trump's order would **bar USPS** from delivering ballots not on a federal voter list.
A federal judge already **blocked it** in nearly two dozen states as unconstitutional.
Trump appealed to the **Supreme Court** on July 27 to let it proceed anyway.
**Vermont's Republican governor** Phil Scott publicly defended mail-in voting against the order.
Arizona's top election official calls it **'unconstitutional'** — and says mail ballots help the GOP too.

depth.background: Since taking office, Trump has pushed to centralize control over how America runs its elections, arguing mail-in voting invites fraud — a claim election officials from both parties say isn't backed by evidence at scale. Earlier this year he signed an executive order directing the Department of Homeland Security to build a **'State Citizenship List'** of eligible voters, barring the Postal Service from delivering ballots to anyone not on it, and encouraging the Justice Department to investigate local election officials who resist. The **US Constitution's Elections Clause** gives states — not the federal government — the primary power to run their own elections, which is the legal basis courts have used to block the order in **nearly two dozen states**.

stories.title: RBI set to hold interest rates steady for a sixth straight meeting even as India's economy runs hotter than expected
stories.what_happened: India's MPC meets from **August 3 to 5**, with the decision due August 5 at 10am IST. The overwhelming consensus among economists — 68 of 72 surveyed by Reuters — is that the RBI will hold the repo rate at **5.25%**, even though early estimates from SBI Research suggest the economy may have grown faster than **7%** in the April–June quarter (Q1 of fiscal year 2026–27), beating expectations. The reason for caution: retail inflation climbed back to **4.38%** in June, above the RBI's 4% target, and the central bank is also watching a wobblier rupee and global trade uncertainty, including fresh US tariffs. Only four of the surveyed economists expect a hike, and none expect a cut.
key_points: The RBI's rate-setting committee meets **August 3–5**, with the decision due **August 5 at 10am IST**
**68 of 72 economists** polled by Reuters expect the RBI to hold the repo rate at **5.25%**
**SBI Research** estimates India's economy could have grown **more than 7%** in the April–June quarter
Retail inflation rose to **4.38%** in June, back above the RBI's 4% target
The hold reflects the RBI balancing **strong growth** against **inflation, a weaker rupee, and global uncertainty**

depth.background: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sets the **repo rate** — the interest rate at which it lends to commercial banks — roughly every two months through its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC). That rate ripples through the economy: it shapes what banks charge on home loans and business credit, and how much they pay savers on fixed deposits. India's central bank has held rates unchanged at 5.25% for months, a level it judges low enough to support growth without overheating prices. Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** has repeatedly said the RBI wants inflation durably near its 4% target before cutting further.

stories.title: Assam's flood death toll climbs to 82 as nearly 2 lakh people remain displaced across five districts
stories.what_happened: According to the Assam State Disaster Management Authority, the flood death toll rose to **82** after two more deaths were confirmed, even as the number of people affected fell to **1.92 lakh** as waters recede in some areas. Flood conditions persist across **Sivasagar, Charaideo, Golaghat, Jorhat and Nagaon** districts, spanning **17 revenue circles and 379 villages**. Charaideo remains the worst-hit district with **77,456** affected people, followed by Sivasagar at **63,492**. The state government is running **54 relief camps** housing nearly **13,000** displaced residents, plus **26 relief distribution centres** serving over **5,000** more people. The floods have also damaged an estimated **15,430 hectares** of farmland, threatening the livelihoods of farmers in the affected belt.
key_points: The flood death toll in Assam has risen to **82**, with **1.92 lakh people** still affected.
**Charaideo** district is worst hit, with **77,456** people affected, followed by Sivasagar with **63,492**.
**54 relief camps** are running, sheltering nearly **13,000** displaced people.
Around **15,430 hectares** of farmland have been damaged, hitting farmers' livelihoods.
Five districts — Sivasagar, Charaideo, Golaghat, Jorhat and Nagaon — remain flood-affected with **379 villages** submerged.

depth.background: Assam floods almost every year when monsoon rains swell the Brahmaputra river and its tributaries, but the scale varies widely year to year depending on rainfall and how early embankments break. The state's **Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA)** tracks deaths and displacement daily during flood season. This year's flooding has already displaced hundreds of thousands of people at its peak and remains one of the deadliest flood seasons Assam has recorded in years, even as the affected population count has started to recede from its highs.

stories.title: The Strait of Hormuz is now effectively shut to shipping as Iran claims more tanker interceptions and oil ticks higher
stories.what_happened: Iranian state media said its forces intercepted **two vessels** attempting to leave the Strait of Hormuz on **July 31**, and claimed four additional tankers turned back after Iranian naval intervention — claims that remain **unconfirmed** by independent trackers. Shipping data firm **Kpler** still recorded a small number of tankers carrying Gulf-loaded oil transiting the strait that day, alongside two other commodity vessels, showing the passage isn't fully sealed even as volumes have collapsed. By **August 1**, daily transits were running at roughly **10 ships**, down from a normal ~88 per day — a near-total shutdown of one of the world's most important trade routes. Kuwait separately said it intercepted a new round of Iranian drone attacks, while a commercial tanker was struck in the strait and left unable to maneuver. Oil prices climbed **more than 1%** on the Iranian claims alone.
key_points: Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has collapsed to roughly **10 ships a day**, versus a normal flow of about **88 ships a day**.
Iran says its forces stopped **two more vessels** trying to exit the strait on July 31, and claims **four other tankers** turned back — though this is unconfirmed.
Shipping tracker **Kpler** still recorded a handful of tankers and commodity vessels crossing, showing the shutdown isn't total or independently verified.
**Oil prices rose more than 1%** on July 31 on the Iranian claims alone, even without confirmation.
The crisis has now run for **over five months**, since it began in **late February 2026**.

depth.background: About a fifth of the world's oil and a large share of its liquefied natural gas normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow chokepoint between Iran and Oman that connects Gulf oil producers to the open ocean. Iran began targeting shipping and, most recently, firing drones directly at Kuwait as its confrontation with Israel and the US widened beyond direct strikes on its own territory. Washington and Israel are separately weighing a joint bombing campaign against Iran's power stations and oil refineries, which could escalate the standoff further.

thread.previously: We reported Iran fired drones at a Kuwaiti government facility and struck a commercial tanker near the Strait of Hormuz, an attack Kuwait condemned as a violation of its sovereignty.
thread.changed: Traffic through the strait has now collapsed to roughly 10 ships a day from a normal ~88, Iran claims further tanker interceptions, and oil prices are responding — turning an attack into what looks like a near-shutdown of the waterway.

stories.title: Verstappen's Red Bull relationship is 'not going smoothly,' Marko admits, as holiday photos with Wolff fuel Mercedes talk
stories.what_happened: Red Bull's long-time advisor Helmut Marko said publicly that the relationship between Verstappen and his engineers 'isn't running smoothly,' citing incidents like the Canadian Grand Prix, where Verstappen said he raced with a setup he already knew wouldn't work, and the British Grand Prix, where he wanted a fresh power unit after qualifying but the team refused. Marko cited Red Bull's inconsistent pace, an unstable car, and this growing tension as obstacles the team hasn't fixed this season. Separately, photos emerged of Verstappen and partner **Kelly Piquet** vacationing with Mercedes team principal **Toto Wolff** and his wife during the summer break — relaxing together on a yacht and riding jet skis — reigniting paddock speculation that Verstappen could eventually move to Mercedes. The timing is notable: it follows Red Bull's $80 million-a-year offer through 2029, which would remove the performance clause that currently lets Verstappen walk away if he isn't at least second in the standings — a threshold he has already missed, sitting sixth, 110 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli, without a win this season.
key_points: Red Bull advisor **Helmut Marko** admitted the Verstappen-Red Bull relationship isn't 'going smoothly'
He pointed to **friction between Verstappen and his race engineers** over car setup at recent races
Photos surfaced of Verstappen and partner Kelly Piquet on holiday with **Mercedes boss Toto Wolff**
It follows Red Bull's **$80 million-a-year** offer through 2029 that would drop his performance exit clause
Verstappen sits **6th in the standings**, 110 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli, without a win all season

depth.background: Max Verstappen has won four straight F1 world titles with Red Bull, but 2026 has been the team's toughest season in years — Red Bull is the only top-four team yet to win a race, and Verstappen's contract includes a performance clause letting him leave early if he isn't at least second in the standings by the summer break. He currently sits sixth. Red Bull recently offered him a new deal worth $80 million a year through 2029 that would remove that exit clause, but Verstappen has not yet accepted it, and speculation about a move to a rival team — especially Mercedes — has simmered all season.

thread.previously: Red Bull tabled a new deal worth $80 million a year through 2029, aiming to keep Verstappen by removing the performance clause that lets him leave if he isn't at least second in the standings.
thread.changed: Marko has now publicly admitted the Verstappen-Red Bull relationship 'isn't running smoothly' over engineering friction, while fresh holiday photos of Verstappen with Mercedes boss Toto Wolff have fueled new speculation he could leave for Mercedes instead of signing the new offer.

stories.title: Esteban Ocon's Haas seat for 2027 is now a 'distant prospect' as his rookie teammate outpaces him
stories.what_happened: Esteban Ocon has scored just **3 points** through Haas's first 10 races of the 2026 season, trailing his rookie teammate Oliver Bearman, who has generally out-qualified him through the year. Haas holds a **team-controlled option** on Ocon's contract for 2027, meaning the decision to retain him rests with the team rather than the driver. A growing list of potential replacements is reportedly under consideration, including McLaren reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli — regarded as a serious contender after impressing in recent testing — as well as Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, Toyota-backed Ryo Hirakawa, Yuki Tsunoda, and Haas reserve Jack Doohan. Ocon has said he has "nothing to announce yet" regarding his future, a statement made as speculation intensified heading into F1's summer break.
key_points: **Esteban Ocon** has scored just **3 points** across Haas's first 10 races of 2026, sitting well behind rookie teammate **Oliver Bearman**.
Haas holds a **team-controlled option** on Ocon for **2027** — meaning the team, not Ocon, decides whether he stays.
A growing list of names — including **McLaren reserve Leonardo Fornaroli** and **Ferrari junior Rafael Camara** — are reportedly in the frame to replace him.
Ocon says he has **"nothing to announce yet"** about his future as speculation builds heading into the summer break.
It's part of a wider driver-market shuffle, with several 2027 seats — including Fernando Alonso's own — still unresolved.

depth.background: Ocon joined Haas for the 2026 season after a difficult, publicly strained exit from Alpine, where he'd raced since 2020. Haas operates on one of the smaller budgets on the grid, making consistent point-scoring especially important for a driver's leverage in contract talks. His teammate, Oliver Bearman, is a rookie promoted through Ferrari's junior program and has generally been quicker across qualifying sessions this season, a gap that reflects poorly on Ocon given his far greater experience.

stories.title: India and China reopen Himalayan border trade routes after a six-year freeze
stories.what_happened: On **August 1**, India and China resumed border trade through all three passes for the first time in six years. In Himachal Pradesh's Kinnaur district, **16 local traders** set off on the first expedition through **Shipki La** towards Shipki village in Tibet, carrying goods on horseback after a ceremonial send-off by Revenue and Horticulture Minister **Jagat Singh Negi**, who presented the traders with traditional ceremonial scarves. Under the trade rules, Indian traders can carry **72 types of items** across, while goods coming back from the Tibetan side are limited to **30 types**; traders must complete their business and return within **72 hours**. Similar resumptions took place at Nathu La in Sikkim and Lipulekh in Uttarakhand.
key_points: Barter trade resumed through **three Himalayan passes** — Shipki La, Nathu La and Lipulekh — on **August 1**
The routes had been shut for **six years**, since 2019, over Covid and heightened border tensions
**16 local traders** carried out the first expedition through Shipki La in Himachal Pradesh's Kinnaur district
Traders can carry **72 types of goods** into Tibet and bring back **30 types**, returning within **72 hours**
Himachal's Revenue Minister **Jagat Singh Negi** flagged off the traders with a traditional ceremony

depth.background: Shipki La, Nathu La and Lipulekh are ancient Himalayan trade passes connecting Indian border communities with Tibet for centuries, long before the modern India-China border existed. Local traders would carry goods across on a **barter system** — no cash changes hands, goods are simply exchanged for goods — sustaining livelihoods in remote mountain districts. Border trade through these passes was suspended in **2019**, first over pandemic restrictions and then because of the sharp deterioration in India-China relations after their **2020 military clash in Ladakh**, which froze most cross-border cooperation for years.

stories.title: Odisha keeps 22 Hirakud Dam gates open as floods hit 8+ lakh people, days before President Murmu's visit
stories.what_happened: Heavy upstream rain pushed inflow into the Hirakud reservoir above **4.15 lakh cusecs**, prompting authorities to open a 22nd gate to release water — keeping inflow and outflow roughly balanced around **3.9 lakh cusecs**, with the reservoir at **625.47 feet**. The resulting discharge has put 10 downstream districts on high alert and affected more than **8.34 lakh people** across 20 districts overall, damaging civic infrastructure and cropland. Chief Minister Mohan Majhi carried out an aerial survey of the hardest-hit areas. The flooding comes just as security is being stepped up in Bhubaneswar ahead of President Murmu's scheduled three-day visit starting August 3, which authorities say remains on track.
key_points: The **Hirakud Dam** — one of the world's longest earthen dams — is discharging floodwater through **22 gates** after inflow crossed **4.15 lakh cusecs**.
The flooding has affected more than **8.34 lakh people (834,000) across 20 districts** of Odisha, damaging homes, roads, and cropland.
**Ten downstream districts are on high alert** as dam authorities balance inflow and outflow to avoid a sharper surge in the Mahanadi river.
The floods come just days before **President Droupadi Murmu's three-day visit to Odisha (August 3–5)**, prompting extra security at Bhubaneswar's railway station.
Odisha Chief Minister **Mohan Majhi conducted an aerial survey** of the worst-hit districts, including Bhadrak, Jajpur, Kendrapara, and Jagatsinghpur.

depth.background: Odisha, on India's eastern coast, sits at the mouth of the Mahanadi river system and floods almost every monsoon season (roughly June–September) when heavy rain upstream forces reservoirs like Hirakud to release water to protect the dam itself — which can flood downstream areas even as it prevents a dam failure. Hirakud, built in the 1950s, is one of the largest earthen dams in the world and is central to flood control for the entire Mahanadi basin. This year's flooding follows Assam's own deadly floods earlier this monsoon season.

stories.title: Two migrant workers from Chhattisgarh shot dead by terrorists at a Kulgam brick kiln in South Kashmir
stories.what_happened: Terrorists attacked labourers at a brick kiln in the Kelam area of Kulgam district, South Kashmir, late on Friday evening. Two workers — identified as **Deepak Ratray and Bopinder**, both from **Chhattisgarh** and in their twenties — were shot. Ratray succumbed to his injuries before he could be taken to a hospital. Bopinder was first rushed to GMC Anantnag and later referred to **SKIMS Hospital in Soura**, where he later died during treatment, taking the confirmed death toll to two. The attack follows closely on an earlier incident less than 10 days prior, in which terrorists allegedly shot and killed a police officer in Anantnag town.
key_points: Terrorists shot two migrant labourers at a brick kiln in **Kulgam district**, South Kashmir, late Friday.
Both victims — **Deepak Ratray** and **Bopinder** — were from **Chhattisgarh** and in their **twenties**.
One died at the scene before reaching hospital; the second died later at **SKIMS Hospital, Soura**, taking the toll to **2**.
The attack comes **less than 10 days** after terrorists shot dead a police officer in nearby Anantnag town.
Migrant workers from outside Jammu & Kashmir have repeatedly been targeted in the region in recent years.

depth.background: Jammu and Kashmir has periodically seen targeted attacks on non-local migrant workers — often labourers from poorer states like Bihar, Chhattisgarh or West Bengal who travel to Kashmir for construction and manual work. Security forces say such attacks are intended to spread fear and disrupt the local economy, which relies heavily on migrant labour for construction and other manual work. The region has been under heightened security since past waves of such killings, but attacks still recur periodically, especially outside the main tourist and urban centres.

stories.title: Israel strikes across Gaza hours after Hamas signs a historic disarmament deal — and Netanyahu's office calls it not enough
stories.what_happened: Less than 24 hours after Hamas's signature on the disarmament framework, Israeli forces launched strikes across Gaza that killed **at least two Palestinians** and wounded **at least ten more**, according to reports from the territory. Israel's government hasn't disputed the deal outright but says its core demand — the **complete demilitarization** of Gaza — hasn't been met, and a senior Israeli official said there would be **no Israeli withdrawal** from the military's current 'yellow line' position until that happens. A **two-week ceasefire window** is nominally in place to work out implementation details; officials have warned that if Hamas doesn't visibly begin disarming, that will be treated as a ceasefire violation. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the agreement 'the only good news in recent days,' underlining how fragile the diplomatic track still is even as strikes continue.
key_points: Hamas **signed** a 15-point disarmament deal in Egypt — a first for the group.
Israeli strikes across Gaza killed **at least 2** and wounded **at least 10** hours later.
Netanyahu's office says the deal **falls short** of full Hamas demilitarization.
Israel says it won't withdraw from Gaza's **'yellow line'** until disarmament is complete.
A **two-week ceasefire** is meant to lock in the details — or collapse.

depth.background: Gaza's war has run since October 2023, and for months the sides have circled a US-brokered ceasefire without a durable deal. On **Thursday, July 30**, Hamas negotiators signed a 15-point disarmament framework with the US-led Board of Peace in **El-Alamein, Egypt** — the first time Hamas has put its name to any agreement to give up weapons. President **Trump** announced it on Truth Social as 'a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas,' but Israeli officials immediately signaled they weren't satisfied. Hamas, for its part, says it will only fully disarm once a **Palestinian state** is on the table — a demand Trump's announcement never mentioned and Israel flatly rejects.

thread.previously: We reported Trump said Hamas had agreed to disarm, but that neither Israel nor Hamas had confirmed it themselves.
thread.changed: Hamas has now formally signed a 15-point disarmament framework, and Israel has responded not with confirmation but with continued strikes and a rejection of the deal as insufficient.

stories.title: Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll puts a deadline on Adrian Newey's rebuild after a nearly winless start to 2026
stories.what_happened: Aston Martin has managed just **one point** through the first 11 race weekends of the 2026 season, a result blamed on both a difficult chassis and Honda's underperforming, unreliable power unit. Honda, insiders say, only had a skeleton team working on the all-new 2026 engine rules early on and had reassigned many of its F1 specialists elsewhere before ramping back up, leaving it to effectively 'run out of time.' Owner Lawrence Stroll has reportedly told Newey and his engineering team he will give them room to fix the car, but with a deadline attached — meaning further management changes are possible if results don't improve. Newey brought **16 upgrades** to the car at the Hungarian Grand Prix as the start of a recovery push, and Honda's chief engineer has confirmed the manufacturer's updated power unit is set to debut after the summer break, following two more races on the current, underpowered spec.
key_points: Aston Martin has scored **just one point** across the first 11 race weekends of 2026
Owner **Lawrence Stroll** has set a deadline for star designer **Adrian Newey** to show real progress
Aston Martin's struggling **Honda power unit** shares the blame, after Honda ran out of time on the 2026 rules
Newey brought **16 upgrades** to the car at the Hungarian Grand Prix, the start of the recovery push
Honda's **updated engine** is due to debut after the summer break, with two more races on the current spec

depth.background: Aston Martin lured Adrian Newey — the designer behind championship-winning cars at Williams, McLaren and Red Bull — away from Red Bull in 2025 with the promise of building a title-contending team from scratch, backed by owner Lawrence Stroll's heavy investment. But 2026 brought a complete regulation overhaul for F1's cars and engines, and Aston Martin's new Honda-built power unit has struggled badly with reliability and performance, leaving the team near the back of the grid instead of fighting at the front as hoped.

stories.title: Violent winds fan a wildfire into the sea near Athens as Greece fights to save a coastal resort
stories.what_happened: A wildfire that broke out on **Friday** near the coastal village of Agios Vasileios, in the Viotia region, tore toward the popular resort town of **Porto Germeno**, about 70km northwest of Athens. By Saturday it had reached the sea, and homes in the area have been damaged. **Winds up to 130 km/h** hampered the more than 300 firefighters on the ground and forced water-dropping aircraft to stand down for safety, with some redirected to a separate, calmer fire in the Peloponnese. Roughly 300 people who had initially ignored evacuation calls had to be rescued by sea after being cut off by the flames. Greek authorities say wildfires have flared in multiple regions this week, including on the island of Crete, and **three firefighters have died** battling the blazes so far.
key_points: **300+ firefighters** battle a blaze at Porto Germeno, 70km northwest of Athens, as it reaches the coastline.
Winds gusting up to **130 km/h** are grounding water-bomber aircraft, crippling the aerial firefighting effort.
About **300 residents** had to be rescued by boat after ignoring an earlier evacuation order near Agios Vasileios.
**Three firefighters have died** across Greece's wildfires this week, including blazes on the island of Crete.
The fire started **Friday** and is one of several burning simultaneously across Greece, stretching resources thin.

depth.background: Greece endures destructive wildfires most summers, driven by tinder-dry vegetation after hot, rainless months and the country's mountainous, hard-to-access terrain. **Climate change is making these fires more frequent and intense** — hotter summers dry out forests faster, and erratic, stronger wind patterns (like this week's 130 km/h gusts) turn small fires into fast-moving infernos that outrun ground crews. Greece has invested heavily in aerial firefighting fleets since deadly 2018 and 2021 fire seasons, which is why grounded aircraft this week is such a serious setback.

stories.title: India's exporters brace for steeper US tariffs as the August 1 trade-deal deadline passes without an agreement
stories.what_happened: Indian and US trade negotiators failed to finalize an interim agreement before President Trump's **August 1 deadline**, meaning Indian exporters now face the prospect of higher tariffs on goods sent to the US. Trump had previously said imports from India could be hit with rates of **20 to 25%** if no deal was reached, while his broader deadline framework threatens **tariffs as high as 35%** for countries without agreements. The talks remain deadlocked specifically over India's refusal to lower tariffs on **agricultural and dairy imports** from the US, while Washington has resisted India's demands for relief on **steel, aluminium and auto tariffs**. Adding to the uncertainty, a US trade delegation is now expected to visit New Delhi only around **August 25** to resume talks — meaning a resolution is unlikely this month or possibly next.
key_points: The **August 1 deadline** for a US-India interim trade deal passed with **no agreement reached**.
Reports say India-bound goods could face tariffs of **20–25%**, with President Trump earlier warning of rates up to **35%** for countries without a deal.
Talks are stuck because India won't open its politically sensitive **agriculture and dairy sectors**, while the US won't budge on India's steel, aluminium and auto tariff demands.
A US trade team is now expected in New Delhi only around **August 25**, pushing any resolution well past this month.
This follows a separate **February 2026** interim deal that had already cut US tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18% — leaving exporters facing a confusing, still-unsettled picture.

depth.background: The US and India have been negotiating a broader bilateral trade agreement for much of 2026, layered on top of an earlier interim deal reached in February that lowered tariffs on Indian goods. Trump has separately imposed a wave of country-by-country tariff deadlines this year — including the 35% Canada tariff and 10% global baseline that took effect this week — as leverage in trade negotiations worldwide. India's refusal to open agriculture and dairy to US imports, a politically explosive issue given the number of Indian farmers involved, has been the central sticking point in the broader talks.

stories.title: Bangladesh's first Test tour of Australia in 23 years begins — without its fastest bowler
stories.what_happened: Bangladesh's Test squad departed for Australia on **August 1, 2026**, beginning what is the team's first Test tour of the country in **23 years**. The tour will not feature strike pacer **Nahid Rana**, who suffered a **Grade 2 side strain** during Bangladesh's second T20I against Zimbabwe on July 17 and has been ruled out of the entire two-match series. Wicketkeeper-batter **Liton Das** will also miss the opening Test, though he's expected to recover in time for the second. Uncapped quick **Musfik Hasan** has been named in the squad as cover. The tour schedule opens with a three-day warm-up match against a Cricket Australia XI at Darwin's DXC Arena from August 6-8, followed by the first Test in Darwin from August 13 and the second, and final, Test in Mackay from August 22.
key_points: Bangladesh departed for Australia on **August 1**, starting its **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**.
Strike pacer **Nahid Rana** is ruled out of the **entire two-Test series** with a Grade 2 side strain suffered against Zimbabwe.
Wicketkeeper-batter **Liton Das** will miss the **first Test** but is expected to be fit for the second.
The tour opens with a **three-day warm-up match** in Darwin (Aug 6-8), before the **first Test in Darwin from August 13** and the second in **Mackay from August 22**.
Uncapped fast bowler **Musfik Hasan** has been added to the squad in Rana's absence.

depth.background: Bangladesh has toured Australia for Test cricket only rarely, and this trip marks the team's **first Test tour there in 23 years** — a landmark for a side still building credibility in the format's toughest conditions. Australian pitches, with their extra pace and bounce, are traditionally the hardest challenge for subcontinent teams, making a fit, in-form fast-bowling attack especially important. Nahid Rana, Bangladesh's quickest bowler, sustained his injury during the second T20I against Zimbabwe on **July 17**, and the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) confirmed on **July 25** that he would miss the tour entirely.

stories.title: Trump's 'hard deadline' tariffs take effect today — 35% on Canada, a 10% baseline on most of the world, and a new 15% ceiling for the EU
stories.what_happened: On August 1, President Trump's tariff regime moves into its latest, and by his own account final, phase. Most countries — including **India, Japan, Vietnam and Taiwan** — settle at a flat **10% tariff** under Section 122. Canada is the conspicuous exception: a **35% tariff** takes effect today after trade talks failed to produce a deal. The European Union instead operates under a separate arrangement struck July 1: a **15% all-inclusive tariff ceiling** that replaces the old rate for the bloc. China remains apart from the rest, still carrying additional Section 301 duties layered on top of whatever baseline applies. Commerce Secretary **Howard Lutnick** called August 1 a 'hard deadline,' while also noting countries can keep negotiating afterward — a sign today's rates could still shift.
key_points: The White House's **August 1 'hard deadline'** for country-specific tariffs arrives today, with officials saying there will be **no further extensions**.
A **35% tariff on Canada** kicks in, while most trading partners — India, Japan, Vietnam, Taiwan — sit at a **10% baseline** rate.
The EU instead gets a **15% all-inclusive ceiling** under a July 1 deal, replacing the old patchwork of duties.
China remains the outlier, still carrying separate **Section 301** tariffs stacked on top of the baseline.
A broader **forced-labor tariff** covering over **80 trading partners** was finalized just days ago, on July 23.

depth.background: Trump's original 'reciprocal tariff' plan from 2025 set country-specific rates as high as 50%, meant to pressure trading partners into new trade deals. In **February 2026, the Supreme Court struck down** the legal basis for those country-specific rates — an emergency law called IEEPA — ruling he couldn't use it this way. That forced the administration to fall back on a blunter law, Section 122, which allows a flat, across-the-board tariff instead of country-by-country rates. Since then, officials have stitched together a patchwork of new bilateral deals and legal justifications, arriving at today's version of the policy.

stories.title: Iran fires drones directly at Kuwait and hits a tanker near the Strait of Hormuz, widening its war beyond Israel and the US
stories.what_happened: Kuwait's Defence Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted **Iranian drones** early Saturday, with explosions residents heard confirmed to be the interceptions rather than impacts. The drones targeted a **government facility and civilian equipment belonging to a private company on Bubiyan Island** in northern Kuwait. Debris from the downed drones caused damage across the country, though officials confirmed **no casualties**. Separately, a commercial tanker was struck near the **Strait of Hormuz** and left unable to maneuver — one in a growing string of attacks on shipping in the waterway. Kuwait's Ministry of Foreign Affairs formally condemned the attacks as a violation of its sovereignty, international law, the UN Charter, and **UN Security Council Resolution 2817**. The attacks come as Washington and Israel finalize plans for a weekend bombing campaign against Iranian energy infrastructure, with President Trump saying he'll be 'hitting them very hard.'
key_points: Kuwait's air defenses **intercepted Iranian drones** targeting a government site and a company facility on **Bubiyan Island**.
A separate tanker was struck near the **Strait of Hormuz** and left unable to move — the latest hit on commercial shipping.
Kuwait's foreign ministry called the attacks a **'blatant violation of sovereignty'** and a breach of a UN Security Council resolution.
No casualties were reported, but debris from intercepted drones caused **material damage** across the country.
The strikes land as the **US and Israel prepare weekend strikes** on Iran's power and oil infrastructure.

depth.background: Iran has been at war with Israel and, increasingly, the United States since fighting escalated earlier in 2026, with US and Israeli strikes repeatedly hitting Iranian targets including near Tehran. Kuwait and other Gulf Arab states host US military bases and sit directly across the water from Iran, which has long threatened that any US strikes launched from their soil would make them targets too — even though Kuwait itself is not part of the war. The **Strait of Hormuz** is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil and a large share of its gas passes through, making any threat to shipping there a global economic concern, not just a regional one.

stories.title: Russia's deadliest strike on Kyiv in weeks kills at least 9 as ballistic missiles hit residential blocks
stories.what_happened: Russia launched a large wave of **ballistic missiles and drones** at Kyiv in the early hours of Saturday, with the first explosions heard just after **1am local time** and blasts continuing in waves until around 3am. At least **9 people were killed and about 27 wounded**, including four children, according to Ukrainian officials. A residential building in the capital's Shevchenkivskyi district was **partially destroyed**, trapping people under rubble, while fires broke out and power was knocked out in several districts. It was the second major attack on Ukraine in 48 hours. Ukraine's military said it hit back overnight, striking **oil refinery infrastructure in Russia's Bashkortostan region**, roughly 1,300km inside Russian territory. President Zelensky again pressed Western allies for more Patriot interceptor missiles, saying delays in deliveries were costing lives.
key_points: Russia fired waves of **ballistic missiles and attack drones** at Kyiv overnight, the **heaviest barrage on the capital in weeks**.
At least **9 people were killed** and roughly **27 wounded**, including children, after a residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district partly collapsed.
Blasts began just after **1am local time** and continued for hours, with **fires and power outages** reported across several districts.
Ukraine says it struck back at **oil refineries in Russia's Bashkortostan region**, more than 1,300km from the border.
**Zelensky** renewed his push for more **Patriot missile interceptors**, blaming delays in Western air-defense deliveries.

depth.background: Russia has bombarded Ukrainian cities nightly for the past week, part of a summer escalation that has already forced NATO jets into the air after a stray missile crossed into Polish airspace. Kyiv, Ukraine's capital and home to about 3 million people, has increasingly become a direct target rather than a secondary one, as Russia mixes cheap decoy drones with expensive ballistic missiles designed to overwhelm the city's Western-supplied air defenses. The war, now in its **fifth year**, still turns heavily on how much air-defense hardware — especially **Patriot interceptor missiles** — the US and Europe are willing to keep sending. Kyiv has been negotiating with Washington for a license to build Patriot interceptors domestically instead of relying on shipments.

thread.previously: We reported Russia hitting Ukraine with a third straight night of strikes, including a missile that crossed into Poland and forced NATO jets into the air.
thread.changed: A new, deadlier overnight barrage of ballistic missiles and drones hit Kyiv directly, killing at least 9 and partially collapsing a residential building — Ukraine's second major attack in 48 hours.
