stories.title: DRC's Ebola outbreak becomes the largest ever recorded in the country, with over 3,600 cases and a 44% death rate
stories.what_happened: As of the WHO's latest data (through **July 30**), the outbreak has recorded **3,605 confirmed cases and 1,587 deaths** — a case fatality ratio of about **44%**, meaning roughly 4 in 9 confirmed patients have died. It has spread from a single health zone to **49 health zones across five provinces**: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, and Tshopo. The most recently completed reporting week recorded the **highest weekly totals of the entire outbreak** — 567 new cases and 296 deaths — meaning the outbreak is still accelerating, not slowing. A smaller, linked cluster in Uganda has recorded two deaths and 18 recoveries, while at least 651 people have recovered in the DRC. Health officials now describe this as the **largest Ebola outbreak the DRC has ever recorded**, and the fastest-growing on record globally.
key_points: **3,605 confirmed cases** and **1,587 deaths** as of July 30 — a **44% case fatality rate**
The outbreak has spread to **49 health zones across five provinces**, from just one zone in April
WHO already declared it a **Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC)** back in May
The worst week yet was just recorded: **567 new cases and 296 deaths** in a single week
It's caused by the rarer **Bundibugyo strain** of Ebola, historically far less common than the usual Zaire strain

depth.background: The outbreak began in the **Mongbwalu health zone** of Ituri Province in eastern DRC and was first confirmed in April 2026. Unlike most past Ebola outbreaks, which are caused by the more familiar Zaire ebolavirus, this one is driven by the **rarer Bundibugyo strain**, which has historically caused smaller, more containable outbreaks — making its scale here unusual. The WHO declared it a **Public Health Emergency of International Concern**, its highest alert level, in mid-May as containment efforts failed to slow it. Eastern DRC's mix of **armed conflict, weak health infrastructure, and high population mobility** has repeatedly made past Ebola outbreaks there hard to stop.

stories.title: Carlos Sainz reveals he wants to race at Le Mans once his Formula 1 career ends
stories.what_happened: Speaking about life after Formula 1, Sainz said racing in the Hypercar class at Le Mans remains a major ambition, while also mentioning the idea of a lower-pressure GT3 campaign with friends. He explained he wants to eventually 'enjoy motorsport from a different position' than the one he's in today, where he carries the responsibility and pressure of delivering results for a team, versus racing purely 'for enjoyment,' which he called 'the coolest sport to do.'
key_points: Sainz says competing in the **24 Hours of Le Mans'** top **Hypercar class** is a major post-F1 ambition
He's also floated a **GT3 campaign with friends**, done for enjoyment rather than results
He joins **Fernando Alonso and Max Verstappen** in openly eyeing endurance racing after F1
The 31-year-old says future racing would be about **enjoyment**, without today's team pressure and expectations

depth.background: Le Mans is endurance racing's most famous event, a 24-hour test of speed and reliability that has increasingly attracted current and former Formula 1 drivers once their single-seater careers wind down. Verstappen has already made high-profile endurance-racing appearances, including at the Nürburgring, and Alonso has long spoken about a Le Mans return, making this a growing trend among F1's biggest names rather than an isolated case.

stories.title: Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon concede Williams won't hit its 2026 targets despite a recovery plan
stories.what_happened: Speaking on Williams' own **Team Torque** podcast, Sainz and Albon gave a sober midseason assessment: the team is making progress behind the scenes, but neither expects a dramatic turnaround once racing resumes at Zandvoort later this month. Sainz was blunt that Williams 'shouldn't expect to suddenly be at the level we want to be' in the second half of the year. With just 11 points and ninth place in the standings at the summer break, the team's priority has shifted from chasing 2026 targets to making sure this season's struggles don't become a recurring pattern into 2027 and beyond.
key_points: Williams sits **ninth in the Constructors' Championship** with just **11 points** heading into the summer break
Drivers **Sainz and Albon** admit the team won't reach its 2026 ambitions in the second half of the season
Sweeping **new 2026 technical regulations** exposed weaknesses that a promising 2025 had papered over
The team is now focused on **not letting the slump become permanent** rather than an in-season turnaround

depth.background: Williams, one of Formula 1's most storied constructors, had been on a genuine upward curve under team principal James Vowles, capped by a strong 2025 season that raised hopes of a real title challenge. Formula 1 reset its technical rulebook for 2026 — new power units and chassis regulations — which shuffles the competitive order and can undo a team's hard-won progress overnight if its car concept doesn't suit the new rules.

stories.title: Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur bans 'championship fight' talk inside the team as the title race hinges on fine margins
stories.what_happened: According to reporting from Italian outlet Gazzetta dello Sport, **Fred Vasseur** has instructed people inside Ferrari not to use the phrase **'world championship fight'** when discussing the team's 2026 season, even as Ferrari remains mathematically in title contention. Vasseur has said publicly that Ferrari's ability to sustain its **current rate of car development** through the second half of the season will determine whether it can mount a serious title challenge, rather than any single big upgrade. He has described the gap to the front of the field as just **'1-2 tenths'** of a second, framing the fight as won or lost in small increments rather than one decisive breakthrough. The comments come as Ferrari enters F1's mid-season **summer break**, a mandatory shutdown period when all teams pause factory work simultaneously.
key_points: Ferrari team principal **Fred Vasseur** has reportedly banned staff from using the words **'world championship fight'** inside the team.
Vasseur says Ferrari's title hopes depend on **sustaining its current development rate** through the rest of the season.
He has said the team is only **'1-2 tenths'** of a second away from the front, a tiny margin in F1 terms.
The approach favors **steady, race-by-race progress** over publicly declaring a title campaign.
This comes as Ferrari enters F1's **summer break**, a mid-season pause when teams regroup and plan upgrades.

depth.background: In Formula 1, being only **'1-2 tenths' of a second** off the pace sounds tiny, but at the sport's highest level that gap is the difference between winning and finishing outside the podium — cars are so finely tuned that fractions of a second separate the front of the grid from the middle. **Ferrari**, one of F1's most historic and pressured teams, has a long history of raising fan and media expectations early in a season only to fall short, which can create internal pressure that some team bosses believe hurts performance. **Fred Vasseur** has led Ferrari since 2023 and has generally tried to manage expectations more carefully than some of his predecessors.

stories.title: Mercedes boss Toto Wolff rules out Verstappen for 2027 — but leaves the door open to pairing him with Antonelli later
stories.what_happened: **Toto Wolff**, Mercedes' team principal, confirmed that **George Russell and Kimi Antonelli** will continue as the team's driver pairing for the **2027 season**, closing the door on any near-term Verstappen move to Mercedes. However, Wolff added that a future **Verstappen-Antonelli partnership** at Mercedes remains a real possibility beyond 2027, saying the team is **'not afraid to make it happen one day.'** The comments come as Antonelli, just **19 years old**, has become this season's breakout star — leading the drivers' championship after multiple wins, including his **sixth win of the season** at the Belgian Grand Prix, ahead of both Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and his own teammate Russell. Verstappen, by contrast, is having an unusually difficult season, sitting **seventh in the standings without a win**, though he remains under contract with Red Bull through **2028** with clauses that could let him leave early depending on performance.
key_points: **Toto Wolff** confirmed **George Russell and Kimi Antonelli** will remain Mercedes' driver lineup for **2027**.
That rules out **Max Verstappen** joining Mercedes next season, despite persistent speculation.
But Wolff said Mercedes would **'not shy away'** from pairing Verstappen and Antonelli together **at some point in the future**.
**Antonelli, 19,** currently **leads the championship**, ahead of Ferrari's Hamilton and teammate Russell.
**Verstappen sits seventh** in the standings, still without a race win this season.

depth.background: Formula 1's driver market runs on a mix of contracts and speculation — teams often lock in lineups a year or more ahead, and rumors about star drivers switching teams are a constant subplot of every season. **Max Verstappen**, a multiple world champion, has been the subject of persistent rumors about leaving **Red Bull**, the team he's driven for his whole F1 career, partly because his current deal is believed to include performance-linked exit clauses. Meanwhile, **Kimi Antonelli**, a 19-year-old Italian driver in only his second F1 season, has emerged as the surprise story of 2026 — leading the championship at Mercedes, the team that famously dominated F1 in the mid-2010s under Wolff's leadership.

stories.title: Trump's new 10-12.5% tariffs on 60 countries — including India — take effect over a forced-labor enforcement dispute
stories.what_happened: The US Trade Representative's office confirmed that new tariffs of **10% to 12.5%** on imports from **60 countries** — spanning Europe, China, and India — took effect on the morning of **August 1, 2026**, after being announced the day before. Together these countries account for **99.4% of everything the US imports**. The administration says the tariffs are a penalty for countries that haven't done enough to stop goods made with forced labor from entering global supply chains. **India's rate was set at 10%**, lower than the 12.5% initially floated. Products like oil, gas and fertilizer are carved out and exempt. This adds to an already tangled tariff picture: Canada saw a separate 35% tariff take effect the same day, and India separately still faces an earlier 25% tariff tied to a different dispute.
key_points: New US tariffs of **10% to 12.5%** on goods from **60 trading partners** took effect on **August 1**, covering **99.4% of all US imports**.
The stated reason is that these countries have **inadequately enforced bans on forced-labor-made goods**, not the usual 'reciprocal trade' justification.
**India's rate was set at 10%**, after initially being floated at 12.5%.
**Oil, gas and fertilizer** shipments are exempted from the new tariffs.
This is separate from — and stacks on top of — the earlier India-specific tariff dispute (25% for India, 19% Pakistan, 20% Bangladesh) from Trump's 'Liberation Day'-style orders.

depth.background: Since returning to office, President **Trump** has repeatedly used tariffs — taxes on imported goods, paid by the importer and usually passed on to consumers — as a negotiating tool on issues ranging from trade deficits to drug trafficking to, now, labor standards. Courts have already pushed back once: in February 2026 the **Supreme Court ruled** that the law Trump used for his broadest 'reciprocal' tariffs (IEEPA) didn't actually give the president that power, striking those down. This new round uses a different legal basis — forced-labor enforcement — to reach a similarly broad set of countries.

stories.title: India seals off a 2,530km stretch of the Indian Ocean for a major missile test expected August 6-7
stories.what_happened: India issued a **Notice to Airmen (NOTAM)** restricting civilian air and sea traffic across a **2,530-kilometre corridor** of the Indian Ocean, from sea level to unlimited altitude, covering **August 6 and 7, 2026**. Defence analysts, based on the size and location of the exclusion zone, believe the test involves either a next-generation **Agni** ballistic missile or the **K-4 submarine-launched ballistic missile**, likely fired from a nuclear submarine such as **INS Arighaat** or **INS Arihant**. The launch is expected to originate near **Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island** off Odisha, India's primary missile-testing site. The stated technical goals include validating **precision guidance systems and multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicle (MIRV) technology**.
key_points: India has issued a **NOTAM (Notice to Airmen)** closing a **2,530-kilometre corridor** over the Indian Ocean to civilian aircraft and ships from **August 6-7**.
Experts believe the test involves either an advanced **Agni ballistic missile** or the **K-4 submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM)**.
The K-4 has a range of roughly **3,500km**; the Agni-V, the other likely candidate, can reach over **5,000km**.
The test is expected to launch from **Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island**, off the coast of **Odisha**, run by DRDO and the Strategic Forces Command.
Goals reportedly include testing **precision guidance and multiple-warhead re-entry** technology.

depth.background: India maintains a **'no first use' nuclear doctrine**, meaning it has pledged not to use nuclear weapons first — but backs that pledge with a credible **second-strike capability**: the ability to retaliate even after absorbing an attack. Submarine-launched missiles like the **K-4** are central to that, because a submarine hidden underwater is much harder for an adversary to destroy in a first strike than a land-based missile silo. India tests these systems periodically from facilities on Odisha's coast, run by the **Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)**.

stories.title: Washington state declares emergency as Western US wildfires explode past 300 square miles amid record heat
stories.what_happened: Washington Governor Bob Ferguson declared a **state of emergency** over the weekend after unusually high temperatures and strong winds fed record wildfires across the state, with more than **312 square miles now burning across 12 large fires**. The declaration frees up state resources — National Guard support, emergency funding, mutual-aid agreements — to help overwhelmed local fire crews. It comes as the broader heat dome pushed Las Vegas to 115°F, just a degree short of its hottest day on record, with similarly extreme readings reported from Arizona up through Montana. Fire risk has also remained elevated in Europe, where wildfires in southwestern France have been 'stabilized' but face renewed danger as temperatures there climb toward 41°C (106°F).
key_points: Washington Governor **Bob Ferguson** declared a state of emergency as record heat and high winds fed the state's fires.
More than **312 square miles** are currently burning across **12 large fires** in Washington alone.
Las Vegas hit **115°F**, just one degree off its all-time daily record.
The same 'heat dome' stretches from **Arizona to Montana**, an unusually wide footprint for a single heat event.
Meteorologists expect the dome to be **relatively short-lived**, but dangerous while it lasts.

depth.background: A 'heat dome' is a large, stubborn zone of high-pressure air that traps hot air underneath it like a lid, pushing temperatures far above normal for days at a time over a wide region. The current one settled over the Western US last week, sending Las Vegas and Phoenix toward all-time highs and drying out vegetation that was already primed to burn after a dry summer. High winds accompanying the heat have made containment far harder for fire crews.

thread.previously: We reported a 'heat dome' pushing Las Vegas to 115°F and Phoenix toward 116°F, warning the extreme heat was spiking wildfire risk across the Western US.
thread.changed: That risk has now turned into a full emergency: Washington's governor has declared a state of emergency as wind-driven fires exploded across the state, and the heat wave has pushed into the Pacific Northwest.

stories.title: Verstappen ends exit speculation, confirms he's racing for Red Bull through the rest of 2026
stories.what_happened: Heading into F1's summer break, **Max Verstappen** put an end to weeks of exit speculation by confirming directly that he will race for **Red Bull** for the rest of the 2026 season, rather than trigger the performance-linked clause in his contract that had become active. He said it had 'always been quite clear' to him that he was staying, dismissing the rumours as unnecessary noise. At the same time, he made clear he expects more from the team, saying Red Bull 'can't take its foot off the pedal' and needs to 'find more performance' as the season resumes at the Dutch Grand Prix. Red Bull remains the only team among the current top four constructors without a race win this year, even with Verstappen's four podium finishes.
key_points: Verstappen says he **will definitely stay** with Red Bull, calling the exit talk unnecessary speculation.
He said it was **'always been quite clear'** to him that he was staying anyway.
Red Bull is the **only top-four team without a win** so far in 2026 despite four Verstappen podiums.
He wants the team to **'find more performance'** heading into the season's second half.
The Dutch Grand Prix, Red Bull's home-adjacent race, is the first stop after the summer break.
The comments come after weeks of paddock talk about friction between Verstappen and the team.

depth.background: Verstappen's Red Bull contract reportedly contains a performance-linked exit clause that becomes usable if the team falls too far off the competitive pace — and 2026 has been Red Bull's roughest season in years, with the team yet to win a race despite Verstappen taking four podium finishes. That drought, combined with reported tension with senior management and holiday photos of Verstappen alongside Mercedes boss Toto Wolff, had fuelled speculation he might use the clause to leave for a rival team.

thread.previously: We reported Verstappen's Red Bull exit clause had become active, and that a pundit read his frustrated Hungarian GP radio messages as a sign he might be angling to leave.
thread.changed: Verstappen has now shut that speculation down directly, saying heading into the summer break that he will definitely stay with Red Bull rather than trigger the clause.

stories.title: India's ₹90,000 crore submarine deal with Germany comes down to how long a boat can hide underwater
stories.what_happened: India and Germany are in the final stages of negotiating a roughly **₹90,000 crore** deal for **six Type-214-derivative submarines**, to be built in India by **Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited** in partnership with Germany's **ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems**. The headline technical detail driving the current coverage is endurance: these submarines can remain continuously submerged for about **three weeks** using AIP fuel cells, and have an overall endurance window of around **84 days** at sea — a major tactical advantage for stealth patrols in the Indian Ocean, where detection risk rises every time a submarine has to surface. The deal would be Germany's first transfer of full submarine-production technology to a non-European partner. German ambassador **Philipp Ackermann** has said the agreement could be finalized within the next month, though as of now **no contract has been signed**.
key_points: India and Germany are closing in on a **₹90,000 crore (about €8 billion)** deal to build **six next-generation submarines** for the Navy.
The submarines use **Air-Independent Propulsion (AIP)**, letting them stay submerged and undetected for **up to three weeks straight**.
Germany's **ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS)** will partner with India's state-run **Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders (MDL)** to build them in India.
It marks Germany's **first-ever transfer** of submarine production technology to a country outside Europe.
German ambassador Philipp Ackermann has said the pact could be **signed within weeks**, though no contract is inked yet.

depth.background: India's submarine fleet is aging, and the Navy has spent years trying to fast-track next-generation boats under **Project-75I**, a program to build advanced diesel-electric submarines domestically under the 'Make in India' push. Modern conventional submarines are judged heavily on how long they can operate without surfacing (which exposes them to detection) — a capability that traditionally required nuclear propulsion. **AIP (Air-Independent Propulsion)** systems let diesel-electric submarines generate power without surfacing for air, closing much of that gap at a fraction of the cost of a nuclear boat. Germany has held informal talks with India on this deal for years, competing against Spain's Navantia for the contract.

stories.title: Haas boss admits his own team is 'fighting with both hands tied' — because it still won't spend up to F1's budget cap
stories.what_happened: Speaking this week, Komatsu confirmed that Haas is still not operating at the full F1 budget cap, despite the cap existing specifically to help smaller teams compete. He pointed to the team's roughly **400-person headcount**, dwarfed by rivals with over 1,000 staff, and to less sophisticated simulator and development equipment. Haas started the 2026 season reasonably well, scoring **18 points** in its first three grands prix, but has managed only **3 points** since and been shut out entirely across the last three races, leaving it seventh in the constructors' championship as midfield rivals like Racing Bulls bring bigger upgrades. Komatsu said raising the funding to properly resource the team is now one of his top personal priorities, framing the issue as a business problem, not a talent problem: "It's not a reflection of our guys; it's more a reflection on my side."
key_points: Haas team principal **Ayao Komatsu** admitted the team still isn't spending up to F1's **budget cap**, unlike its rivals.
Haas runs with roughly **400 staff**, compared to over **1,000** at some bigger midfield teams.
The team scored **18 points in its first three races** this year but just **3 points since**, and none in the last three events.
Komatsu says funding the team properly — not driver or engineer talent — is now 'one of the top priorities' on his job list.
He described the situation bluntly: Haas is **'fighting with both hands tied'** against better-resourced rivals.

depth.background: Formula 1 introduced a **budget cap** in 2021 to level the financial playing field between giant manufacturer-backed teams and smaller independents — every team is allowed to spend up to the same ceiling on car development each year. In theory, this should let a smaller team like **Haas** compete evenly with bigger-budget rivals. In practice, a team still has to actually raise enough sponsorship and revenue to spend up to that cap — the rule sets a ceiling, not a floor. Haas has historically run leaner than almost any other team on the grid, which helped it survive financially but has increasingly left it out-developed as rivals pour resources into new-regulation cars.

stories.title: A review of 350+ studies suggests the protein craze may be overselling what most people actually need
stories.what_happened: The review, released July 31 and covered widely on August 1, concludes that reducing protein intake improves metabolic function, lowers inflammation and cellular damage, and activates pathways linked to healthier aging. A central mechanism is **FGF21 (fibroblast growth factor 21)**, a hormone that rises when protein intake falls; mice with elevated FGF21 levels lived longer than typical mice in prior studies. The researchers point to three amino acids in particular — methionine, isoleucine and valine — as likely drivers of protein's downside, since overloading these can switch on growth-signaling pathways associated with obesity and age-related disease. The authors are careful to caveat that this isn't a blanket recommendation: older adults, athletes, and people recovering from illness or surgery generally still need more protein, not less.
key_points: A review spanning **more than 350 studies** finds many people — especially sedentary adults — eat **more protein than they need**, and that eating less may slow aging.
The effect runs through a hormone called **FGF21**, which rises when protein intake drops and is linked to **longer lifespans in mouse studies**.
Three amino acids — **methionine, isoleucine and valine** — appear to drive much of protein's downside, over-activating growth pathways tied to inflammation and disease risk.
The finding mainly targets **sedentary people**; older adults, athletes and those with certain medical conditions may still need higher protein intake.
It runs against the grain of the booming **high-protein diet and supplement industry**, built on the premise that more protein is almost always better.

depth.background: Protein has been marketed for years as the nutrient you can't get enough of — protein bars, shakes and high-protein diet plans have turned into a multi-billion-dollar industry on that promise. But nutrition science works on dose-response curves: past a certain point, more of a 'good' nutrient can start working against you. Researchers, including scientists like **Dudley Lamming** who study aging and metabolism, pooled findings from over 350 individual studies — a method called a systematic review — to see what the overall evidence on protein and aging actually shows once you look past marketing claims.

stories.title: OpenAI's unreleased 'Astra' model solves 10 math problems that stumped humans for decades
stories.what_happened: OpenAI announced on August 1 that Astra, a model not yet publicly released, produced verified solutions to ten open problems spanning group theory, coding theory, geometry, complexity theory and quantum game theory. Standout results include constructing the **first non-sofic group** (disproving the Connes rigidity conjecture), proving Ehrhart's volume conjecture, and improving the best-known bound on high-dimensional sphere-packing density for the first time since 1978. Astra also proved a parallel repetition theorem for two-player quantum games and set new lower bounds on how hard it is to compute a mathematical object called the permanent. Every proof shipped with a **Lean 4** certificate — a format that lets a separate, simple computer program mechanically verify the logic is airtight, rather than requiring a human referee to trust it. OpenAI says generating all ten proofs cost **under $2,000** in compute.
key_points: OpenAI's unreleased **Astra** model solved **10 long-standing open problems** in math and theoretical computer science that had resisted progress for **at least a decade**.
It disproved the **Connes rigidity conjecture** and built the first known **non-sofic group** — a counterexample mathematicians had chased for years.
Astra delivered the **first improvement since 1978** to a key upper bound on how densely spheres can be packed in high dimensions.
OpenAI published a **249-page manuscript** with machine-checked proofs (Lean 4 certificates) for every result, and says the compute cost was **under $2,000**.
The haul includes three problems from mathematician **Paul Erdős's** famous open-problem list — a sign AI may now do genuine, independently checkable research, not just pattern-matching.

depth.background: For years, AI models have been good at mimicking known math — solving textbook problems or summarizing proofs others already found. Genuinely *new* mathematics, the kind that extends human knowledge, has been a much higher bar, because a wrong proof is worse than no proof at all. OpenAI says its next-generation model, internally called **Astra**, has cleared that bar on ten problems that professional mathematicians had failed to crack for **a decade or more**, including a famous conjecture by mathematician Alain Connes and a sphere-packing bound untouched since **1978**. The company avoided a 'trust us' problem by publishing formally verified proofs anyone can independently check.

stories.title: Lando Norris says driving better than his title year but sitting fifth 'hurts' — but he's not giving up
stories.what_happened: Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix, his first win of the season, but still sits fifth in the drivers' standings on 128 points, well behind leader Kimi Antonelli (219) and second-placed Lewis Hamilton. He said his personal driving this season has been stronger than during his title-winning 2025 campaign, which makes trailing in the standings more frustrating — in his words, it 'hurts.' He added he would 'believe for as long as possible' rather than write off the season, even as McLaren's technical team has reportedly been up to three months behind rivals in adapting to 2026's new rules.
key_points: Lando Norris says it 'hurts' to be driving **better than during his 2025 title-winning season**, yet not have the car to show for it in 2026.
Despite winning the **Hungarian Grand Prix**, Norris sits **fifth in the standings on 128 points** — **91 points behind** championship leader Kimi Antonelli's 219.
Norris insists he'll 'believe for as long as possible' that defending his title is still mathematically alive, refusing to concede the season early.
McLaren has been as much as **three months behind rivals** in developing to F1's all-new 2026 technical rules.
His comments add to a wider grumble among senior drivers this season that F1 is prioritizing '**entertainment**' over pure racing authenticity.

depth.background: Norris won the 2025 Formula 1 drivers' championship with McLaren. A sweeping rules reset for 2026 — new engines and car regulations — reshuffled the competitive order, and McLaren has struggled to adapt as quickly as rivals like Mercedes and Ferrari, leaving the reigning champion team well off the pace for much of the first half of the season. 'Mathematically alive' means Norris's points deficit, while large, still isn't so big that a title defence is technically impossible with races remaining — though in practice it requires him to significantly outperform the championship leader from here.

stories.title: Mercedes plots a 'more sizeable' F1 upgrade for after the summer break to fend off Ferrari
stories.what_happened: Mercedes deputy technical director Simone Resta said the team is 'clearly focused on trying to develop the car at every event, but also trying to think bigger with bringing another step on the car' after the summer shutdown. The team has already brought incremental upgrades earlier in the season, including at Silverstone, but Resta signaled the post-break package will be a genuine step change rather than another small tweak, timed for F1's return at the Dutch Grand Prix in late August.
key_points: Mercedes says it's targeting a **bigger upgrade package** after F1's summer break, aiming to have it ready for the **Dutch Grand Prix** in late August.
Deputy technical director **Simone Resta** said the team wants something 'more sizeable' on the car, not just incremental tweaks race to race.
The push is aimed at fending off championship rival **Ferrari**, whose faster in-season upgrade pace has worried Mercedes engineers.
It comes despite Mercedes driver **Kimi Antonelli leading the 2026 drivers' championship** with a commanding points lead heading into the break.
Under F1's all-new 2026 technical rules, teams are still chasing performance — a big midseason step can meaningfully swing the title fight either way.

depth.background: 2026 brought a **major regulation reset** for Formula 1 — new engine rules and car design constraints that reshuffled which teams are fast, similar to past rule-change years that flipped the competitive order overnight. That reset is why Mercedes, despite leading the championship through rookie-ish standout Kimi Antonelli, isn't resting: an early-season points lead built partly on rivals' slow starts can evaporate if a competitor's car simply gets faster as the season goes on. Ferrari has been bringing upgrades at a quicker pace this year, which is what's driving Mercedes' urgency.

stories.title: Modi opens Andhra Pradesh's Bhogapuram airport and breaks ground on the state's first semiconductor plant
stories.what_happened: On August 1, PM Modi inaugurated the **Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport at Bhogapuram**, near Visakhapatnam — a GMR-built project costing more than **₹5,640 crore**, designed to handle **6 million passengers a year** in its first phase (expandable to 40 million), with commercial flights beginning **August 17, 2026**. During the same visit, Modi laid the foundation stone for the **ASIP Semiconductor Project** in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh's first chip-manufacturing plant — a joint venture with South Korea's APACT, approved under the India Semiconductor Mission, with reported investment figures ranging from roughly ₹460 crore to ₹2,500 crore depending on the source. In total, Modi unveiled projects worth more than **₹17,900 crore**, also covering power-transmission lines and highway infrastructure in the state.
key_points: PM Modi inaugurated the **Bhogapuram International Airport** near Visakhapatnam, built by GMR at a cost of over **₹5,640 crore**.
The airport is designed for **6 million passengers a year** in its first phase, expandable to **40 million** — commercial flights start August 17.
Modi also laid the foundation for the **ASIP Semiconductor Project**, Andhra Pradesh's first chip-manufacturing plant, a joint venture with South Korea's **APACT**.
The chip plant falls under India's **Semiconductor Mission**, the government's push to build domestic chip-making capacity.
The visit unveiled a total package of over **₹17,900 crore** in projects, including energy transmission and highway infrastructure.

depth.background: India has spent the last few years trying to cut its reliance on imported semiconductors — the tiny chips that power everything from phones to cars — by incentivizing domestic fabrication and packaging plants under the **India Semiconductor Mission**. Andhra Pradesh has been positioning itself as a hub for both aviation and electronics manufacturing in South India, alongside established hubs like Gujarat and Tamil Nadu. The Bhogapuram airport, structured as a public-private partnership with infrastructure firm GMR, has been years in the making as the region's answer to congestion at Visakhapatnam's existing airport.

stories.title: Argentina Women beat Canada Women to go 3-0 up in a rare cricket series in South America
stories.what_happened: Argentina Women, captained by **Maria Castiñeiras**, defended a total of just **96/9** to beat Canada Women (captained by Rabbjyot Rajput) by **18 runs** in the 4th T20I of a seven-match series, bowling Canada out for **78** in 18.4 overs. Player of the match **Alina Emch** top-scored for Argentina with **17 off 18 balls** and then took **3 wickets for 16 runs** with the ball. It was Argentina's third straight win, giving them an unassailable **3-0 series lead** — they had already won the opener on July 29 by a dramatic 1 wicket, with Julia Andujar and Francesca Galan steering the chase home. Two more matches were scheduled for August 2 itself.
key_points: Argentina defended a modest **96/9** to bowl Canada out for **78**, winning by **18 runs**.
**Alina Emch** was player of the match, scoring 17 off 18 balls then taking **3 wickets for 16 runs**.
The win gives Argentina an **unassailable 3-0 lead** in a seven-match T20I series.
Argentina had already won the series opener by a dramatic **1 wicket** on July 29.
The series is being played in **Buenos Aires**, a country with almost no cricketing tradition.

depth.background: Cricket is a minor sport in South America, where football dominates, but the International Cricket Council (ICC) has been funding development in 'associate' nations — countries without full Test status — to grow the game's global footprint. Argentina and Canada are both ICC associate members building up their national teams ahead of qualifying tournaments for global events like the Women's T20 World Cup. This series, played on Argentina's home turf, is part of that development effort.

stories.title: UEFA tells FIFA president Gianni Infantino: resign, or face a no-confidence vote
stories.what_happened: UEFA announced on **Saturday, August 1** that it had lost confidence in Infantino and was demanding change, after his £15bn World Cup stake-sale plan collapsed under internal opposition. UEFA's 55 member nations are reportedly prepared to vote Infantino out if he doesn't resign first — and UEFA alone can trigger the process, since only 43 nations are needed to force an extraordinary FIFA congress. Concacaf piled on with its own statement calling the stake-sale plan an 'egregious act of poor governance and leadership.' England's Football Association publicly backed UEFA's position. FIFA staff are reportedly calling the internal rebellion 'kill the monster.'
key_points: UEFA, backed by **all 55 of its member federations**, is threatening to force Infantino out via an emergency no-confidence vote.
The trigger: Infantino was forced to **scrap a £15 billion plan** to sell a stake in World Cup commercial rights after a revolt inside FIFA.
Only **43 member nations** are needed to force the vote — UEFA alone clears that bar.
Concacaf, the North/Central American federation, separately accused Infantino of an **'egregious act of poor governance.'**
FIFA insiders reportedly nicknamed the internal revolt **'kill the monster.'**

depth.background: Gianni Infantino has led FIFA, world football's governing body, since **2016**, steadily centralizing power and drawing criticism for a governing style critics call autocratic — including cozying up to political leaders like Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. FIFA's confederations — regional bodies like UEFA (Europe) and Concacaf (North/Central America) — are technically Infantino's political base, but each holds voting power that can be turned against him. The immediate spark was Infantino's plan to privately sell a stake in FIFA's commercial arm, effectively monetizing part of the World Cup's rights, worth a reported **£15 billion**.

stories.title: FBI investigates possible Iran-linked hackers after cyberattacks hit water systems in Michigan and Minnesota
stories.what_happened: Minnesota disclosed earlier this week that cyberattacks had struck more than **30 of its water systems**. Michigan followed on **August 1**, confirming intrusions at nine of its own utilities. The FBI confirmed it is investigating both states' breaches but stressed no attacker has been formally identified. Officials are examining whether the intrusions trace to **Iranian state-linked hackers**, consistent with last week's warning, though they caution the attacker could also be someone else deliberately mimicking Iranian techniques to inflame the US-Iran standoff. Local operators say every affected system kept running safely, with no reported impact on drinking-water safety.
key_points: Michigan reported cyberattacks on **nine water systems**, days after Minnesota reported breaches at over **30 utilities**.
The FBI is investigating whether **Iranian hackers** are behind the intrusions, but has not confirmed attribution.
Investigators are also checking whether attackers **faked Iranian fingerprints** to stir panic during the US-Iran conflict.
All affected systems **kept operating safely** — no contamination or health risk has been reported.
The breach follows a **joint FBI/CISA warning** that Iranian hackers were targeting US water-sector control systems.

depth.background: For years, US water utilities — often small, local, and short on cybersecurity budgets — have been a favorite target for state-linked hackers because they run **industrial control systems** (the computers that open valves and run pumps), which are easier to breach than a bank or power grid. Iran-linked groups have hit American water utilities before, including a 2023 wave that defaced Israeli-made equipment. Tensions have escalated sharply since the US and Israel struck Iranian targets and Iran began attacking tankers in the **Strait of Hormuz**. Last week, the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned that Iranian-linked hackers were actively probing water-sector controls.

stories.title: RBI overhauls fixed-deposit interest rate rules — banks must publish bulk rates daily and stop favoring select customers
stories.what_happened: The RBI finalized new deposit interest rate rules that take effect from **October 1, 2026**. Banks must now charge the **same interest rate to all customers** for deposits of a similar size accepted on the same day — including bulk deposits of ₹3 crore or more, typically used by corporates, institutions, trusts, and high-net-worth individuals rather than retail savers. Banks will also be required to publish their bulk deposit rates on their websites by **10:00 am each business day** (with a 10-minute grace period), and are barred from quoting a different rate to another customer once that rate is published. The rules cover commercial banks, small finance banks, regional rural banks, payment banks, local area banks, and urban co-operative banks.
key_points: New rules take effect **October 1, 2026**, under RBI's 'Amendment Directions 2026.'
Banks must offer the **same interest rate to every customer** for similar deposits made on the same day — no more special rates for favored clients.
**Bulk deposits (₹3 crore or more)** — used mainly by companies and wealthy individuals, not ordinary savers — are most affected.
Banks must **publish their bulk deposit rates online by 10:00 am** every business day (10-minute grace period allowed).
The rules apply to **commercial banks, small finance banks, regional rural banks, payment banks, and co-operative banks.**

depth.background: Fixed deposits (FDs) are one of the most common ways Indians save money — you lock cash with a bank for a fixed term in exchange for a guaranteed interest rate. For large ('bulk') deposits, banks have historically been able to negotiate different rates with different customers behind closed doors, which regulators worry lets banks quietly favor big corporate clients in ways ordinary depositors can't see or match. The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, India's central bank, regulates how banks price these deposits.

stories.title: India scraps toll booths on the Gurugram-Jaipur highway, switching to pay-as-you-drive-through tolling
stories.what_happened: From **August 1, 2026**, the entire 270-km Gurugram-Jaipur stretch of NH-48 is barrier-free. NHAI completed the rollout by upgrading the last plaza, Shahjahanpur in Rajasthan — the Daulatpura and Manoharpura plazas had already switched over earlier. The system uses high-performance **RFID readers** paired with **Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR)** cameras mounted on gantries above the road. As a car passes underneath at highway speed, the gantry reads its FASTag and plate, and the toll is deducted automatically from the linked FASTag account — no braking, no queue.
key_points: The **270-km stretch** of National Highway-48 between Gurugram and Jaipur now has **zero toll barriers**.
The last holdout, the Shahjahanpur plaza in Rajasthan, went barrier-free on **August 1**, completing the corridor rollout.
The new system, called **MLFF (Multi Lane Free Flow)**, reads your FASTag and number plate at full driving speed — no stopping.
Toll is deducted **automatically from your FASTag** as you pass beneath a gantry, not a physical booth.
NHAI plans to extend this to **all four-lane-plus highways by March 2029**, per the government's Economic Survey.

depth.background: India rolled out **FASTag** — a prepaid RFID sticker that lets cars pay tolls without stopping — nationwide back in 2021, but drivers still had to slow down at a barrier that only lifted after the tag was scanned. That created bottlenecks anywhere traffic was heavy or a tag failed to scan. The **National Highways Authority of India (NHAI)** has been testing a barrier-free alternative called MLFF, which drops the physical gate entirely and instead uses overhead cameras and RFID readers to bill moving vehicles directly.

stories.title: Hamburg's Pride parade draws 300,000 under doubled security, a week after the deadly Berlin attack
stories.what_happened: Hamburg's Pride parade — one of Germany's largest — went ahead on Saturday, August 1, exactly a week after the Berlin attack, with police roughly doubling the officer presence compared to last year. Around **300,000 people** turned out, more than the 260,000 who attended in 2025, suggesting the attack did not deter attendance. The event's motto was 'Queer in solidarity — take a stand for a future without fear,' and organizers added a truck representing the Berlin Pride event to the parade as a show of solidarity. This came as German authorities continue to face scrutiny over how Ballout — twice flagged for extremism, including a 2025 conviction tied to ISIS — remained free to carry out the attack.
key_points: Around **300,000 people** attended Hamburg Pride, up from 260,000 last year, despite the recent attack.
Police roughly **doubled the number of officers** protecting the event compared to last year.
It came exactly **one week** after a van-and-blade attack killed one person and injured 29 at Berlin's Pride festival.
A truck representing **Berlin's Pride event** was added to the Hamburg parade as a gesture of solidarity.
Investigators say the Berlin attacker had pledged allegiance to **ISIS** in a video found after his death.

depth.background: On July 25, a 21-year-old German-Lebanese man, Abdul Ballout, drove a van into pedestrians near Berlin's Christopher Street Day festival, killing one woman and injuring 29 before being shot dead by police the next day. German prosecutors later confirmed it as **Islamist terrorism** and revealed Ballout had two prior convictions tied to extremism — including a suspended sentence — despite being known to authorities. The attack triggered a national debate over how Germany monitors people already flagged as security risks, and put pressure on the government to overhaul event security nationwide.

thread.previously: We reported that German prosecutors confirmed the Berlin Pride van-and-blade attack was Islamist terrorism, detailing attacker Abdul Ballout's history of ISIS-linked convictions despite being known to authorities.
thread.changed: A week later, Hamburg held its own Pride parade under doubled security and drew a bigger crowd than last year, in a visible show that the community would not be intimidated out of public events.

stories.title: Assam floods death toll climbs to 80 as government announces a six-month loan moratorium for affected families
stories.what_happened: Assam's flood death toll rose to **80** as of the latest count, with over **2.12 lakh people** affected across eight districts. More than 16,500 people displaced by the floods are currently staying in 71 relief camps, while over 72,000 additional people are receiving relief through distribution centres. In response, the Assam government announced a **six-month moratorium on loan repayments** for anyone in flood-affected districts, covering all types of loans, and has begun distributing free replacement textbooks to students whose books were destroyed. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall continuing over Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland for the next three days, meaning the crisis is not yet over and water levels could rise again.
key_points: Assam's flood death toll has risen to **80**, with over **2.12 lakh people** affected across eight districts.
More than **16,500 displaced people** are living in 71 relief camps; 72,000+ more are getting relief supplies.
The state government announced a **six-month moratorium** on loan repayments for people in flood-hit areas.
IMD has forecast **more heavy rainfall** over the next three days, raising fears of renewed flooding.
Neighbouring Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland are also battling flooding and landslides from the same rain system.

depth.background: Assam floods almost every monsoon season because the Brahmaputra river and its tributaries swell rapidly with heavy rain from the surrounding hills, and low-lying, densely populated districts have little natural drainage. This year's flooding has been especially severe, compounding damage from earlier flooding and landslides that hit Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland through late July. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has already met MPs from the affected northeastern states and pledged continued central assistance, while Union Home Minister Amit Shah has reviewed the situation twice in a week.

stories.title: Aston Martin's Lawrence Stroll names Carlos Sainz his 'top target' to replace Alonso — with design chief Adrian Newey reportedly pushing the move
stories.what_happened: Multiple reports say Lawrence Stroll has now specifically named **Carlos Sainz** as Aston Martin's 'top' target to replace Fernando Alonso, should the two-time champion leave the team. Crucially, the push reportedly has three layers of internal backing: Newey has **personally recommended** prioritising Sainz over other options, the move has Stroll's own support, and Alonso himself is said to have encouraged Aston Martin to go after Sainz before stepping back from the succession decision. Sainz's own contract situation makes this live now — he is due to be out of contract with Williams at the end of 2026 unless he takes up an option for 2027 or 2028, and he has said he intends to decide his plans during the summer break. Much of that decision, Sainz says, will depend on how much Williams' upgrade package — due at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix — improves the car's competitiveness.
key_points: Aston Martin owner **Lawrence Stroll** has identified Williams driver **Carlos Sainz** as his top target if Fernando Alonso leaves.
Design chief **Adrian Newey** has reportedly personally recommended Aston Martin prioritise signing Sainz.
Alonso himself is said to have **encouraged** the move before stepping back from team decisions.
Sainz is out of contract with Williams at the **end of 2026** unless he exercises an option for 2027/2028.
Sainz says his decision partly hinges on gains from Williams' **upgrade package** due at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

depth.background: Aston Martin has struggled through a nearly winless start to the 2026 season despite bringing in Newey — F1's most decorated car designer — and Honda power, prompting Stroll to put a deadline on the team's rebuild. Fernando Alonso has repeatedly said he'll decide his own F1 future during the summer break, while shutting down suggestions he could return to Alpine. Carlos Sainz, who lost his Ferrari seat to Hamilton for 2025 and moved to Williams, has been the subject of driver-market speculation for over a year, with rivals like Aston Martin long circling him as a potential signing.

stories.title: Spain's Ceuta migrant crisis death toll surges to 67 as tens of thousands are pushed back to Morocco
stories.what_happened: Between **Thursday and Friday (July 30-31)**, roughly **60,000 migrants rushed the Ceuta border fence** from Morocco in one of the largest mass-crossing attempts in the enclave's history. Spanish officials now say the **confirmed death toll has risen to 67**, with people killed in a **stampede at a breakwater barrier** extending into the sea and others drowning trying to swim around fencing. Spain's Prime Minister visited Ceuta after the crisis broke, and the government has begun building a **500-meter sea barrier** to close off the water route. **More than 48,000 of those who crossed have already been sent back to Morocco**, though officials say the border still isn't fully under control days later. Death toll figures have varied by outlet (41 to 67) because of the difficulty confirming which recovered bodies are linked to the crossing.
key_points: Confirmed **death toll has climbed to 67**, up sharply from the 18-19 first reported on July 31.
About **60,000 migrants breached the border fence** into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in a single stretch.
**48,000+ have already been pushed back** into Morocco as authorities scramble to regain control.
Spain is installing a **500-meter sea barrier** at the breakwater where many died in a stampede.
Death toll figures have varied across outlets (41-67), reflecting the chaos of confirming bodies.

depth.background: Ceuta is a small **Spanish territory on the North African coast**, separated from mainland Morocco only by a fence and a strip of water — one of just two land borders between Africa and the European Union. It's long been a flashpoint for migration, because reaching it means setting foot on EU soil without a Mediterranean boat crossing. Spain and Morocco jointly police the border, and mass rushes like this happen when thousands try to cross the fence or swim around it at once, overwhelming guards. **Morocco's cooperation with Spain on border control is a major, sometimes tense, pillar of their relationship**, and incidents like this test it.

thread.previously: On July 31 we reported at least 18 dead after tens of thousands of migrants stormed the Ceuta border fence from Morocco.
thread.changed: The confirmed death toll has jumped to 67 as more bodies are recovered, and Spain has begun building a permanent sea barrier while pushing back over 48,000 people to Morocco.

stories.title: FIA closes Mercedes' engine loophole from today, targeting the championship leader mid-season
stories.what_happened: After weeks of dispute between rival manufacturers and the FIA, F1's governing body confirmed a **mid-season rule change** closing the compression-ratio loophole, effective **1 August 2026**. From now on, engines must comply with the compression limit not just when cold, but also at a **representative 130°C operating temperature** — closer to real racing conditions — which is expected to strip away the advantage Mercedes had found. The change required support from at least four of the five power unit manufacturers and was ultimately **approved unanimously** by the FIA's World Motor Sport Council, alongside a minor tweak to the qualifying format. Because the rule takes effect during the summer break, the **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort** on 21 August will be the first race run under the new standard.
key_points: A new rule takes effect from **1 August 2026**, closing a loophole Mercedes was believed to be exploiting in engine rules.
Power units must now meet the **compression ratio limit** at a hot **130°C operating temperature**, not just at rest.
The change needed **4 of 5 engine manufacturers** to vote in favour — it passed **unanimously** at the World Motor Sport Council.
Mercedes-powered cars, including championship leader **Kimi Antonelli**, have held **10 of 11 poles** this season.
**Zandvoort's Dutch Grand Prix**, the first race back from the summer break, is the first event affected by the change.

depth.background: Formula 1 introduced all-new engine ('power unit') regulations for 2026, lowering the maximum **compression ratio** — a measure of how much an engine squeezes its fuel-air mixture before ignition, which affects power and efficiency — from 18.0 to 16.0. Rivals suspected Mercedes had found a way around the spirit of that limit: compliance was only checked when the engine was cold and not running, and Mercedes was believed to be exploiting the gap between that resting measurement and how the engine actually performs once hot, during a race. Mercedes has dominated 2026 so far, with **teenage sensation Kimi Antonelli** the youngest-ever leader of the F1 drivers' championship.

stories.title: China holds military drills near Scarborough Shoal after the Philippines files a UN claim over the reef
stories.what_happened: The Philippines this week formally deposited an official nautical chart with the **United Nations**, defining the normal baselines of Scarborough Shoal and the outer limits of its 12-nautical-mile territorial sea and 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. China's **People's Liberation Army Southern Theatre Command** responded on Saturday by staging joint air and naval combat drills in the waters and airspace around the shoal. In a statement, the Southern Theatre Command called the Philippine baselines **'illegal and invalid'** and said the drills were necessary to safeguard China's 'territorial sovereignty and maritime rights.' China's foreign ministry separately said Scarborough Shoal is China's 'inherent territory.' The drills came just days after the Philippines ran **joint maritime exercises with the US and Japan** in the same area.
key_points: China's military ran **joint air and naval drills** around Scarborough Shoal, days after the Philippines filed a **UN seabed claim** over the reef.
The **Philippines** submitted official nautical charts to the UN defining **territorial-sea baselines** around the shoal under international maritime law.
China's **Southern Theatre Command** called the Philippine move **'illegal and invalid'** and vowed a resolute response.
The drills follow **joint US-Japan-Philippines exercises** in the same waters days earlier.
China has held **effective control** of the shoal since a tense **2012 standoff**, despite a 2016 international tribunal ruling against its wider claims.

depth.background: Scarborough Shoal is a triangle of rocks and reefs in the South China Sea that both China (as Huangyan Dao) and the Philippines (as Bajo de Masinloc) claim as their own. China seized effective control of the shoal after a **2012 standoff** with Philippine vessels and has patrolled it with coast guard and naval ships ever since, despite a **2016 international tribunal ruling** that rejected China's broad claims to the South China Sea. The shoal sits within the Philippines' 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone but is more than 800km from the Chinese mainland. Tensions have flared repeatedly in recent years over Chinese coast guard vessels blocking and water-cannoning Philippine boats near the reef.

stories.title: RBI likely to hold interest rates again this week as strong growth collides with monsoon-driven inflation risk
stories.what_happened: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets **August 3-5**, and **SBI Research expects it to leave the repo rate unchanged** for a sixth straight meeting — even though India's GDP growth for the April-June quarter is tracking **above 7%**, stronger than expected. The reasoning: **inflation risk is rising**, not falling. Consumer price inflation is estimated to have climbed to roughly **4.4% in June**, with analysts flagging a **weak monsoon and elevated Brent crude prices** as upside risks to food and fuel costs. Separately, India's monsoon has actually **improved through July**, cutting the nationwide rainfall shortfall to **13%** from a much deeper deficit earlier in the season — a mixed signal that eases some, but not all, of the inflation worry. One forecast even sees the RBI needing **50 basis points of rate increases later in 2026** if these pressures build.
key_points: RBI's rate-setting committee meets **August 3-5**, with most analysts expecting rates to be **held steady, not cut**.
SBI Research forecasts this despite India's economy **growing faster than expected** in the April-June quarter.
**Monsoon rainfall has recovered**, cutting the nationwide shortfall to just **13%** after a weak start to the season.
Consumer inflation is estimated to have risen to around **4.4%** in June, with food-price risk still on the table.
One forecast sees **50 basis points of tightening later in 2026** even if August brings no change.

depth.background: The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** is India's central bank, and its **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** meets roughly every two months to set the **repo rate** — the rate at which it lends to commercial banks, which ripples through to loan and deposit rates across the economy. The RBI balances two goals that often pull in opposite directions: keeping **inflation** near its target (around 4%) while supporting **economic growth**. A weak or erratic **monsoon** (India's June-September rainy season) matters hugely here because it drives crop output — and therefore food prices, the biggest single component of Indian inflation.

stories.title: India's GST collections jump 15.4% to a record ₹2.11 lakh crore in July, driven by a surge in import taxes
stories.what_happened: The government released July's GST numbers on **August 1**, showing gross collections of **₹2.11 lakh crore, a 15.4% year-on-year jump**. Growth wasn't even across the board: **revenue from imports surged 28.8%** to ₹66,511 crore, while **domestic collections — from sales inside India — grew a more modest 10.1%** to ₹1.45 lakh crore. After the government paid out GST refunds, **net revenue for the month came to ₹1.81 lakh crore, up 15.8%** from a year ago. This is the **second time in the current financial year (FY27)** that monthly collections have topped the ₹2 lakh crore mark, a threshold seen as a sign of a healthy, high-consumption economy.
key_points: **Gross GST collections hit ₹2.11 lakh crore** in July, up **15.4%** from a year earlier.
**Import-linked GST revenue jumped nearly 29%** to ₹66,511 crore, far outpacing domestic growth.
**Domestic GST collections rose 10.1%** to ₹1.45 lakh crore.
After refunds, **net GST revenue rose 15.8%** to ₹1.81 lakh crore.
This is only the **second month this fiscal year** collections have crossed the ₹2 lakh crore mark.

depth.background: **GST (Goods and Services Tax)** is India's single nationwide indirect tax, charged on most goods and services sold, which replaced a patchwork of state and central taxes when it launched in 2017. The monthly GST number is one of the most closely watched **real-time gauges of India's economy** — because it's collected almost immediately after a sale happens, it shows how much buying and importing is actually going on, well before slower official GDP data arrives. The finance ministry releases this figure on the **1st of every month** for the previous month's collections.

stories.title: India opens a ₹4,000 crore credit line for Bhutan's energy projects as ties deepen
stories.what_happened: India's Foreign Secretary **Vikram Misri** concluded a two-day visit to Bhutan's capital, Thimphu, during which the two countries signed a **₹4,000 crore** concessional Line of Credit agreement between India's Export-Import Bank and Bhutan's finance ministry, earmarked for energy projects. Misri and his Bhutanese counterpart, **Dasho Pema Lektup Dorji**, co-chaired the fifth round of India-Bhutan Development Cooperation Talks, covering Bhutan's ongoing 13th Five-Year Plan. The two sides also approved **12 new projects** worth a combined ₹332 crore. Officials described the credit line as separate from and additional to India's existing ₹10,000 crore support package for Bhutan's current five-year plan, which runs from 2024 to 2029.
key_points: India signed a **₹4,000 crore concessional Line of Credit** with Bhutan, dedicated to **energy projects**.
The deal was signed during Foreign Secretary **Vikram Misri's** two-day visit to Thimphu.
The two countries also approved **12 new development projects** worth ₹332 crore.
It's **separate from** India's existing **₹10,000 crore** support package for Bhutan's current Five-Year Plan (2024-2029).
The credit line carries **below-market interest rates**, making it cheaper for Bhutan to borrow than through commercial lenders.

depth.background: Bhutan is one of India's closest strategic partners, sandwiched between India and China in the Himalayas, and India has long been its largest aid donor, trading partner, and hydropower investor. India has funded major hydropower plants in Bhutan for decades, buying the electricity back to help meet its own power needs while giving landlocked Bhutan a crucial source of export revenue. Delhi treats close ties with Thimphu as strategically important given Bhutan's position along a stretch of the disputed India-China border, including near the sensitive **Doklam plateau**, where Indian and Chinese troops faced off in 2017.

stories.title: India's August money rules kick in: a new nationwide KYC system and revised LPG prices
stories.what_happened: From August 1, **CKYC 2.0** goes live as the formally upgraded version of India's shared KYC framework, described as a move toward a 'One KYC' system. It uses real-time APIs and secure OTP-based consent so that once a customer's identity is verified with one institution, a bank, insurer, or fund house can pull the same verified record instantly using just a mobile number or PAN card — instead of asking the customer to resubmit documents each time. On the same day, IOCL, HPCL and BPCL announced their monthly revision of **domestic and commercial LPG cylinder prices** for brands like Indane, Bharat Gas and HP Gas; because the change depends on international crude and LPG benchmark prices and the rupee's exchange rate, actual new prices differ by city. The changes land alongside several other rules that reset on the 1st of the month, including revised Tatkal railway ticket booking procedures and ITR (income tax return) late-filing penalty deadlines for salaried employees.
key_points: **CKYC 2.0** — a single, shared identity-verification record for banks, insurers and mutual funds — formally launches today, August 1.
It replaces repeated paperwork with **real-time, OTP-based verification** using just your mobile number or PAN.
State-run oil firms **IOCL, HPCL and BPCL** revise domestic and commercial LPG cylinder prices today, as they do on the 1st of every month.
The changes track **international crude and LPG benchmark prices** plus the rupee's exchange rate, so the new price varies by city.
They arrive alongside a wider bundle of 1st-of-the-month changes, including new **Tatkal train-ticket booking rules** and an ITR-filing penalty deadline.

depth.background: India has long required customers to submit the same identity documents separately to every bank, insurer, and mutual fund they deal with — a process called KYC ('Know Your Customer'), meant to prevent fraud and money laundering. A **Central KYC Registry (CKYC)**, run by an RBI/SEBI/IRDAI-backed body, already lets institutions share a customer's verified records, but the system has been clunky. LPG (cooking gas) cylinder prices, meanwhile, are reviewed and adjusted every month by India's state oil marketing companies based on global fuel costs — a routine but closely watched process because gas costs affect nearly every household budget.

stories.title: England captain Sophie Devine ruled out for the rest of The Hundred 2026 with a calf injury
stories.what_happened: **Sophie Devine** injured her calf while attempting to take a catch early in Birmingham Phoenix's run chase during Welsh Fire's defeat on Saturday, and she spent the rest of that match off the field. She has now been **ruled out for the remainder of The Hundred 2026**. Ireland all-rounder **Orla Prendergast** has been named as her replacement in the Welsh Fire squad and was available for the team's following fixture against Southern Brave. With Devine unavailable, Australian leg-spinner **Georgia Wareham** has taken over as **Welsh Fire's captain** for the rest of the competition.
key_points: **Sophie Devine**, Welsh Fire's captain, is **out for the rest of The Hundred 2026** with a calf injury.
She was hurt attempting a catch during Welsh Fire's loss to **Birmingham Phoenix** on Saturday.
Ireland all-rounder **Orla Prendergast** replaces her in the squad.
Australian leg-spinner **Georgia Wareham** takes over as **Welsh Fire captain** for the rest of the season.
The injury is a blow for Welsh Fire, who lose both their **captain and a senior batter** mid-tournament.

depth.background: **The Hundred** is England's short-form domestic cricket competition, played in 100-ball innings rather than the more traditional 20-over (120-ball) format, and it runs as parallel men's and women's tournaments each August. Teams are packed with a mix of English internationals and star overseas players signed for just this one tournament, so a single injury to a captain or senior player can significantly reshape a team's season, since replacements are drawn from a smaller reserve pool than in international cricket. **Sophie Devine**, a veteran New Zealand international, has been one of the most consistent all-format players in women's cricket and was leading **Welsh Fire** this season.

stories.title: Bangladesh's envoy to India says Dhaka 'will not become a playground' for China or Pakistan against Indian interests
stories.what_happened: In an interview with **Deccan Chronicle**, Bangladesh's high commissioner to India, **Muhammad Riaz Hamidullah**, sought to calm Indian unease over Dhaka's outreach to Beijing and Islamabad, saying Bangladeshi soil **'will never be used against Indian interests by anyone'** and that India remains Bangladesh's **predominant trading partner**. He acknowledged that the 2024 uprising and Bangladesh's participation in China's **Belt and Road Initiative** had created an impression of drift between the two neighbours, but argued the China relationship itself was **not new**. Hamidullah also raised **irregular migration**, saying Bangladesh is ready to take back any of its nationals confirmed to have entered India illegally, while asking India to also address the **trafficking networks** that enable such migration, and he invited **Indian universities, tech, and agritech firms** to invest in Bangladesh. The interview surfaced around the same time India's outgoing envoy to Dhaka separately said relations would move **'constructively'** once Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman **visits India** — an invitation from PM Modi that Dhaka has said it is still **reviewing**.
key_points: Bangladesh's high commissioner **Muhammad Riaz Hamidullah** said Dhaka is mindful of India's security concerns and **'will not become a playground for anyone else.'**
The reassurance comes as Bangladesh's new **BNP government under PM Tarique Rahman**, elected in **February 2026**, deepens engagement with **China**, including Belt-and-Road-linked projects.
Hamidullah called Dhaka's relationship with China **'not new'** and instead pitched for **more Indian investment**, saying Indian firms were ceding ground to European companies in Bangladesh.

The remarks land alongside a **separate reassurance from India's outgoing envoy** that ties will move forward **'constructively'** once PM Rahman visits India — an invitation Dhaka is still **reviewing**.

Relations have been strained since the **2024 uprising** that ousted Sheikh Hasina, who has since taken shelter in India, with India summoning Bangladesh's envoy as recently as **late 2025** over security concerns.

depth.background: India-Bangladesh ties were close under Sheikh Hasina's Awami League government but **fractured after a mass uprising forced her from power in August 2024**; she has lived in India ever since, and Dhaka has sought her return to face charges, an unresolved sore point. An **interim government led by Muhammad Yunus** ran Bangladesh until a general election on **February 12, 2026**, which the **Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)** won in a landslide, installing **Tarique Rahman as prime minister** on February 17. Since taking office, Rahman's government has pursued a self-described **'Bangladesh first'** foreign policy — engaging China and, more cautiously, Pakistan — which has fed Indian anxiety about a neighbour drifting into **Beijing's orbit**, a concern India has long framed using the idea of a Chinese **'String of Pearls'** of influence around it. Ties hit a low point in late 2025 when India summoned Bangladesh's high commissioner over security concerns.

stories.title: Table-topping Jaffna Kings, already through to the playoffs, face bottom-placed Dambulla Sixers today as the Lanka Premier League's group stage wraps up
stories.what_happened: Jaffna Kings have been the form team of the tournament, winning five of seven games to top the table and already banking a playoff berth, with **Towhid Hridoy** — signed only as a late replacement — playing a key role in two rapid cameos since joining. Dambulla Sixers, by contrast, have won just once in six games and sit at the bottom, having lost their last three matches in a row, including a defeat to Colombo Kaps earlier this week. Ahead of today's meeting, Dambulla brought in Zimbabwe all-rounder **Sikandar Raza** as an injury replacement, while other franchises reshuffled too: Galle Gallants (currently top of the table on the back of a strong campaign) lost Australian batter Chris Lynn to injury and let Mehidy Hasan Miraz depart early, bringing in Australia's Thomas Rogers as cover. With the playoffs — an Eliminator and Qualifier 1 on August 5, Qualifier 2 on August 7 and the final on August 8, all at the Premadasa Stadium in Colombo — now just days away, today's result and net run rate could still shape who finishes where.
key_points: **Jaffna Kings** sit top of the 2026 Lanka Premier League table with **5 wins from 7 games (10 points)** and have already secured a **playoff spot**.
**Dambulla Sixers** are bottom of the table, having won just once in six games, and must beat Jaffna today and hope other results fall their way to have any hope of survival.

Bangladesh batter **Towhid Hridoy**, brought in only after teammate Taskin Ahmed withdrew, has hit **35 off 21 and 31 off 8** in his first two Jaffna innings — form that helped drag the team off the bottom of the table.
Multiple franchises made **late squad changes** this week: Dambulla added Zimbabwe's **Sikandar Raza**, while Galle Gallants lost **Chris Lynn** (injury) and **Mehidy Hasan Miraz** (early departure).
The **LPL playoffs** begin August 5 at the R. Premadasa Stadium in Colombo, with the final set for August 8.

depth.background: The **Lanka Premier League (LPL)** is Sri Lanka Cricket's flagship T20 franchise tournament, a shop window that mixes international stars with young Sri Lankan talent and returned this year after a two-year hiatus, with the 2026 season opening on July 17. Six franchises play a round-robin, and the **top four** advance to a knockout stage. Because overseas players in T20 leagues are often on short-term deals tied to their national team's schedule, squads change constantly mid-tournament — as seen this week with several franchises swapping players in and out just before the final round-robin fixtures. Today's Dambulla vs Jaffna match at **Pallekele International Cricket Stadium** is effectively the last item of unfinished business before the playoff picture is set.

stories.title: India's judo team wins a fourth Commonwealth Games medal as Unnati Sharma battles to bronze in Glasgow
stories.what_happened: On day 9 of the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, Unnati Sharma won bronze in the women's -63kg judo category, taking India's judo medal tally at these Games to four. She began with an ippon victory over Eswatini's Lamulela Magagula in the round of 16, then narrowly beat New Zealand's Qona Christie by waza-ari in the quarter-finals to reach the last four. In the semi-final she lost by ippon to Australia's Saya Middleton, who went on to win silver, dropping Sharma into the bronze-medal playoff. She won that decisively, defeating South Africa's Skye Knoester by ippon in just **one minute and seven seconds**. Two teammates, Karanjit Singh Maan (men's -90kg) and Harsh Tokas (men's -81kg), reached their own bronze-medal contests today but both lost, ending their medal hopes.
key_points: Unnati Sharma wins **bronze in the women's -63kg** category, India's **fourth judo medal** of the 2026 Games.
She opened with an **ippon win** over Eswatini's Lamulela Magagula, then edged New Zealand's Qona Christie in the quarter-finals.
A semi-final loss to eventual silver medallist **Saya Middleton** of Australia sent her into the bronze playoff.
She sealed bronze with an **ippon in just 1:07 minutes** over South Africa's Skye Knoester.
Teammates **Karanjit Singh Maan** and **Harsh Tokas** both fell just short of the podium in their own weight categories today.

depth.background: Judo has historically been a minor medal source for India at the Commonwealth Games, with the contingent traditionally built around athletics, wrestling and boxing. That changed at Glasgow 2026: judokas **Asmita Dey and Harsh Singh** had already won India's first-ever Commonwealth Games judo golds earlier in the Games. Unnati Sharma, competing in the women's -63kg category, was part of a young judo squad hoping to build on that breakthrough. In judo scoring, a full point (ippon) wins a bout outright, while lesser scores (waza-ari) can add up — meaning matches can turn in seconds.
